subtopic: MR. GARSON    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORTS OF REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JULY 24

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon, Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The Ottawa Citizen and the Ottawa Journal in their evening editions of yesterday, July 25, 1956, have both attributed to me assertions which I did not make-indeed almost the exact opposite of what I made-in debate in this house on July 24, 1956. The Citizen said this:
Justice minister Garson has told the Commons that pollution of the Ottawa river could be controlled or eliminated through the Criminal Code.
The Journal said:
Pollution of the Ottawa river could be eliminated or controlled through prosecutions under the Criminal Code of Canada, Justice minister Garson has advised the Commons.
What I actually said, as reported at page 6388 of Hansard, was this:
As I have stated on previous occasions on which we have considered this matter, I do not think a satisfactory solution to this problem can be found by proceedings in the criminal courts. That, of course, has been the view of the government all along and it is still our view.
I concluded my remarks with a review of the progress that had been made in controlling the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river during the past year and then, as reported at page 6392 of Hansard, I said this:
I think, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend himself will agree-
I was referring to my friend the hon. member for Prince Albert.
-there is more in that one statement-
That is the statement I have quoted of the progress that had been made in the preceding year.
-in the way of progress in the control of the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river than my hon. friend can achieve in a dozen criminal prosecutions, whether under the existing law or under the amendment which he has moved and which I think is totally unnecessary.
The hon. member for Prince Albert had urged the house to amend the common nuisance section of the Criminal Code to make it possible to prosecute a corporation which puts into the North Saskatchewan river at Edmonton a polluting material which, flowing down that river into the province of Saskatchewan, creates a common nuisance in Prince Albert. He asked for support for this amendment upon his allegation that under the present law the corporations located in Edmonton within the jurisdiction of the courts of Alberta could not be prosecuted in those courts for the indictable offence of a common nuisance which they had created in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, within the jurisdiction of the Saskatchewan courts. I opposed the hon. gentleman's amendment upon the ground that section 419 (b) of the new code provides as follows:
For the purposes of this act . . .
I am just reading the relevant words.
. . . where an offence is commenced . . . within one territorial division and completed within another, the offence shall be deemed to have been committed in any of the territorial divisions.
A territorial division includes a province.
This is not only the law now but in a somewhat different wording it has been the law for many years before the new code was passed. The corresponding section of the old code was section 584.
But because it is possible to prosecute a corporation or municipality which commits a common nuisance by putting a polluting effluent into a river, either an interprovincial

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Privilege
river or a river wholly within one province, it does not follow that a series of prosecutions under such a law is necessarily an effective method of controlling or eliminating pollution. Indeed, we have always taken the position that it is not and that the proper method is to prevent pollution by concerted action of the municipalities and governments concerned.

MR. FLEMING    ALLEGED CHANGES IN "HANSARD" BY MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday afternoon following a remark made by the Minister of Defence Production, I made certain comments based upon his statement. These are found at page 6439 of Hansard. I will not read them all, but only one or two. I said, as reported in the second column on that page:
The explanation given by the minister to this committee this afternoon was that this-
That was the sum of $2,880,000 that was paid as a profit to Sorel Industries Limited. -was paid to Sorel Industries Limited because that company was asked to keep its plant in idleness but available for military production if required.
The minister denied that that statement was true and also denied having made the statement that I attributed to him and on which I based my remarks. I added, Mr. Speaker, "that is what the minister said if the record stands as the minister made his statement this afternoon".
Now, the statement that Hansard attributes to the minister in this regard reads as follows at page 6433 of yesterday's proceedings:
it-
That is speaking of the plant of Sorel Industries Limited.
-was closed down in 1945. Very valuable machinery was available there and when it was quite obvious that we would require guns for the Korean crisis we of course were anxious to make an arrangement with Sorel that the machinery would be kept intact for that purpose.
That is what Hansard says the minister said, but Hansard is not correct. What the minister did, in fact, say is as follows:
It was closed down in 1945. Very valuable machinery was kept there and when it was quite obvious that we would require guns for this year we of course were anxious to make an arrangement with Sorel that this machinery would be kept intact for that purpose.
I draw to your attention the fact that there are important differences between the statement the minister made and the statement attributed to him in the Hansard record at page 6433. I draw your attention to the fact that my statement, based upon the minister's statement, was quite justified in relation

to the actual remark the minister made, for the year referred to was the year 1945.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: MR. FLEMING    ALLEGED CHANGES IN "HANSARD" BY MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: He was talking about 1950.

maintopic: MR. FLEMING    ALLEGED CHANGES IN "HANSARD" BY MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: We were talking about-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: MR. FLEMING    ALLEGED CHANGES IN "HANSARD" BY MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: He was talking about 1950, and "this year" refers to 1950.

maintopic: MR. FLEMING    ALLEGED CHANGES IN "HANSARD" BY MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Apparently the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) is now going to jump in and change what was said. What was said was:
It was closed In 1945.
The minister then goes on to talk about "this year". There was nothing said by the minister in that sentence about the Korean crisis, which came in 1950. The whole of the discussion was as to when this company was asked to keep its plant available for the government. There is the whole point, and I draw your attention to the fact somebody has changed the record of what was actually said yesterday.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. I may have misunderstood him the other day when he spoke on the subject of pollution, but I did understand him to say that the present Criminal Code and the provisions thereof would meet the situation in prosecutions against wrongdoers polluting streams, and I thought the report to which he objected was substantially correct. In order to clarify it, however, I would ask the minister whether in his opinion under the provisions of the Criminal Code as they now are prosecutions could be taken in regard to what is taking place on the Ottawa river in particular whereby the waters are being so terribly polluted. Does he believe that under the law as it now exists prosecutions could take place successfully?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING PROSE- CUTION UNDER CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask my hon. friend to clarify his question? Prosecutions for what?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING PROSE- CUTION UNDER CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Prosecutions for pollution under the law as it now exists.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING PROSE- CUTION UNDER CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is surely aware that we have not been discussing pollution in these present debates. We have been discussing the creation of a common nuisance through pollution, which is a very different thing from the mere act of pollution.
If I may reply to his question in terms of the common nuisance we have been discussing, then I would say, confining it to the North Saskatchewan river-and the same thing would apply to the Ottawa river if the circumstances were the same-that where a corporation or a municipality puts a polluting effluent into an interprovincial river, which effluent flowing down the river creates a common nuisance in another province, if those who are interested in prosecuting can get sufficient evidence to bring home this common nuisance that has occurred, let us say, in Prince Albert, to the corporations which put the effluent in the river in Edmonton, then under the new Criminal Code as it now stands, and indeed as it stood before we recently revised it, it is quite possible procedurally to launch a prosecution in Edmonton for the common nuisance that was created in Prince Albert.

I think I have answered the questions I was asked.

When the committee rose at six o'clock yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I had been asking a series of questions about matters pertaining to the administration of this department. We had reached the point where the minister was answering a question I had asked about orders in council and the minister's orders issued under the Defence Production Act. From the table which the minister had before him it is quite clear that no orders have been issued under this act since June 1, 1954, and that the orders in council that had been made prior to that time have all been allowed to lapse. I do not intend to launch into a long discussion on that particular subject, except to point out that it is the clearest kind of answer to the case which the government put up in this house a year ago when asking for continuation without limitation of the absolute powers that were vested in the governor in council and in the minister by that act. They have given their own answer now. The government have not found it necessary to pass a single order in council since June 1, 1954; every order in council that had been made prior to that time has been allowed to lapse and is not in effect; and the minister's orders under that act, as we see from the table the minister has before him, have likewise expired. Clearly, a great deal that was said last year by the government on the subject of the necessity of the continuation of these powers, without any trammelling or limitation, has been proven now to be utterly without foundation.
I come now to the question of house construction carried on through this department and its agencies. I should like to ask the minister how many housing units were constructed during, let us say, either the calendar year or the fiscal year on whatever basis it may be made up, and what was the cost of the housing?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Department of Defence Production does not build houses in cities. We build accommodation up around
67509-410J
Supply-Defence Production the mid-Canada line and some remote areas, but the agency responsible for building housing for the armed forces is Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

Does the minister say that Defence Construction Limited is not taking any responsibility in connection with the construction of housing for the armed forces? My understanding has been that, while they farmed that work out to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, nevertheless the residual responsibility rested with Defence Construction Limited which is, of course, responsible to the Minister of Defence Production.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the responsibility was transferred from the Minister of Defence Production to the Minister of Public Works some years ago by an order in council prepared by myself. We always try to get the agency most capable of doing the work given the responsibility for it.

May we take it that Defence Construction (1951) Limited now has no responsibility whatever in connection with any program for construction of housing quarters for the armed forces or for any government enterprise or agency that is responsible to the Department of Defence Production?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Except, as I said, there is some housing required in connection with stations on the mid-Canada line and also stations on the "Pinetree" line. What we are providing there is accommodation. We do not provide separate housing, but we do provide accommodation at isolated points on projects of that type for which we take full responsibility.
That is not married quarters in any sense; that is just for individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

There are several other specific questions I should like to ask in regard to last year's expenditures. If the minister will turn to page 170 in the book of estimates, there are several items there about which I should like to ask.
The first total is the sum of the salaries for full-time positions. The next line reads, "less anticipated savings due to staff turnover, $200,000." This is an increase of $60,000 over the estimate for the year before, which was $140,000. Can the minister make some comment on the rapidity of turnover in this department. That seems to indicate that there are going to be more savings due to staff turnover, which I presume means more vacancies in the course of the turnover. We

Supply-Defence Production were given to understand last year that if the department were put on a permanent footing, it would dispose of the uncertainty of employment of the members of the staff and result in greater stability within the staff. Will the minister explain this increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, a great number of our officers are technical men, particularly engineers. The turn-over in engineers does not arise from any lack of security in their government jobs. It arises from the fact that employers outside of government pay them twice as much as we do. We are constantly losing key personnel. This is one of the great difficulties. We recently lost the director of our aircraft division. I believe he was offered about 2i times what we were paying him. [DOT] This $200,000 is an estimate of the vacant positions we will have on an average during the year.

My point was, does the increase in the estimate in this respect indicate that more staff turnover is expected in this fiscal year than occurred in the last fiscal year? Is this problem of the loss of technical personnel becoming greater?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, it becomes more serious every month. The demand for trained personnel is terrific and the salaries paid by private industry to get top, key men astonishes me. I thought I was hardened a bit to engineer's salaries, but I must say the modern generation's estimate of them is much higher than I ever thought.
The next item is two lines down, "Less salaries of Employees of Cloth Warehouse, $116,468." What is the explanation of that deduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is charged to the operation of the revolving fund. We have a markup on our cloth covering the cost of warehousing and the cost of the salaries of the people engaged in the warehouse are charged to that item.
The form of the estimate indicates that this is a new type of deduction. Has there been a change in the method of dealing with this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It does not represent a change in the system. It has been suggested that previously it was done by a transfer at the end of the year. In other words, we obtained from the cloth account an amount equivalent to the payment of this commission, but we are not sure of that. We would need to explore that a little more fully. It is an accounting matter and I would want to get the accountant's view. In any case, we have always charged the
IMr. Fleming.]
cost of operating the cloth warehouse to the revolving fund and made a countercharge in the sale price of the cloth to cover it.
The next question is about an item two lines farther down, "living allowances", indicating an increase from $85,000 last year to $90,000 this year. Could the minister explain that increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, that covers the allowances for offices abroad. There are new offices in the United States, somewhat larger offices in England and on the continent. It is a supplement to the salaries that are paid to people abroad.
I take it that this increase is attributable to either the enlargement of the staff or the opening of new offices abroad for purchasing personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is really due to opening offices at Dayton, Ohio, and Philadelphia; more personnel in the United States.
It is for purchasing personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, purchasing or selling; one or the other. Most of our aircraft orders or orders for electronic equipment come from Dayton which is the headquarters of the United States air force and Philadelphia is the purchasing centre for the navy.
Then, three lines farther down we have an item, travelling expenses, $200,000. May I ask what was the actual expenditure in the last fiscal year ended March 31, 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: What is the reason for the contemplated increase this year, then? Is there going to be more travelling done? I thought the indication was that probably now the work of the department in relation to defence had been well advanced and there would probably be less of this type of work to do than in recent years.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, that is not the case. I think our work this year was at the peak of all the years, taking into account the mid-Canada line. It is not so much the volume of the work as where the work is located. This is an estimate by our staff of the probable amount required to cover travelling expenses. If we do not need it we return it to the treasury.
The last item on the list is "Sundries, $90,000". I ask what it covers and what was the actual expenditure last year on the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It was $64,992. The item provides for unforeseen and other items which do not come under the headings of special categories.
Can the minister be a little more specific as to the sort of thing that the sum of $64,992 was expended on in the last fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, I can give that information. Provision for 16 impressed accounts last year amounted to $15,250; services of Dun and Bradstreet, $725; payments to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation re disposal of scrap, $10,000; payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation of one-quarter of one per cent of the value of NATO procurements, surcharged by procurement services, $35,000; social security payments in France, $1,800; miscellaneous, $27,225.
Does the minister contemplate an increase in the expenditures of that type during this fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is what we expect. The figures I just read out are what we expect. That is the allocation for this year. The hon. member wanted the actual expenditures last year?
Yes, I thought that was what the minister was reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, the proposed expenditures for 1956-57.
What do they aggregate? Is that the aggregate of $90,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.
But last year the actual expenditure was $64,992.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. The items I have given are the break-down of what we expect: the impressed account; we always use Dun and Bradstreet a bit in connection with our work; disposal of scrap, the same as last year. I understand that is warehouse charges in connection with scrap. Then, we pay Canadian Commercial Corporation for their procurement services for NATO work, procurement outside the usual department responsibilities; social security for our people in France, and the miscellaneous item for further items that cannot be anticipated but they do crop up.

I think this is where questions on the Canadian Commercial Corporation would be asked. I am just curious about the statement for the year 1956. I notice that interest earned is $96,635. I am just wondering what is the basis for charging interest in this corporation?
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is interest earned on bank balances. The money is often paid, for instance, on procurement for the United States, which is a very big item. Usually the payments are made before the- the Canadian Commercial Corporation pays the producer for the items. With respect to "Pinetree", for example, money was moved up in large amounts in anticipation of expenditures on the program.

In the expenditures I notice contributions to employees' superannuation, death benefits and unemployment insurance totalled $21,995 in 1955, which is the first year the item appears in the accounts; and in 1956, it is $14,251. Does that mean that it will probably level off about there from now on?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, that is what we expect. We do not anticipate enlarging the staff of the Canadian Commercial Corporation. It seems to be about right for the business it is doing.

With respect to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, I notice this item in the statement this year, "Provision for bad and doubtful accounts outstanding for five years or more, $45,157". Does that cover all accounts outstanding over five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am not sure. The Auditor General approves the manner in which the accounts are set up. I presume it is the equivalent of a businessman's provision for bad and doubtful debts. I daresay some of them will be collected. That often happens in business, I know. I cannot say other than that I can make inquiry about it later and find out for the hon. member.

Actually, I would like to know how that amount of $45,157 is arrived at and the exact accounts going to make up that amount. I notice that it was charged to the expenses only this year. In other words, there had not been a reserve of any kind previously to March 31, 1955, and I am just interested in getting some of the details.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I shall be glad to bring that down; I shall have to consult the accountants of the company.

Mr. Chairman, there is
another item in the expense account on page 30 of this statement that I am interested in, namely, "Amortization of costs of office partition, $13,205". In the previous year it was $3,877. I am just wondering why the word "amortization" is used there? I do not see any amount as deferred assets in the balance sheet.
6474	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told it is the normal way of dealing with changes in leased premises; in other words, the changes which have to be paid for by the tenant are written off against the balance sheet in the year in which they occur.
In other words, the full cost is charged in the year in which it is spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I believe so, yes.
Amortization is hardly the right word.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: These are all short-term leases. It is expected that when the new building on Wellington street is finished Crown Assets will then occupy government quarters, but for the past two or three years it has been occupying leased quarters, I think, in two different locations.

Mr. Chairman, on this section I should like to ask one or two questions with regard to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. The corporation handles almost everything, apparently, as seen from this report, from aircraft and so on to land and buildings. In particular, I would like to know how material for disposal comes into the hands of the corporation from the defence services? Do the defence services declare the material surplus to their establishment and notify the corporation to that effect and then hand it over to them? What is the method by which the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation gets control of material from defence services?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The only manner in which anything comes into the custody of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation is through a declaration of surplus by an authorized officer of some branch of government.

I was interested in the arms and ammunition which apparently has been declared surplus to establishment by the services, and has gone into the hands of the crown corporation. Looking back over the last five years I find that some of the surplus equipment has been disposed of by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. For example, in 1950 they disposed of a substantial number of Browning machine guns and parts but in the year 1954-55-I am going by the fiscal year ending 1954-55-surplus pistols, automatic guns, Colt shell guns, rifles and cartridges ball have all been disposed of by International Firearms Limited or Sumac Industries or Ansco Products Company.
I presume these companies perhaps bid for the material that is available from Crown Assets. I do not know, but I would like to follow that up with this question. On page 16


of the report of the department there is a paragraph concerning ammunition which indicates that production of complete rounds of ammunition increased in both volume and variety in 1955. If that is the case and if ammunition is still being produced for the services, how would it become surplus in 1955 and disposed of to the International Firearms Company in the amount of just under 400,000 rounds or cartridges ball as shown in the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation annual report for March 31, 1955, on pages 20 and 21? If the services require ammunition what type of ammunition are they declaring surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Department of Defence Production would not know why the ammunition becomes surplus. All we know is that we have a declaration showing a certain amount of ammunition and its location and it is declared surplus to requirements. We do not go back of that declaration; there is no reason why we should, really. The hon. member said the disposal is carried on also by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. That is not a fact. The Canadian Commercial Corporation acts as procurement agent for foreign governments and NATO. Any ammunition they take on is to fill an order from NATO or from another government. Any declaration of surplus comes to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and is acted on by them.

I understand that. I mentioned the Canadian Commercial Corporation as having, I judge, purchased from Crown Assets certain Browning machine guns in 1950 perhaps on behalf of a foreign government.
I also appreciate the fact that Crown Assets does not know why material is declared surplus to establishment but there is an overlapping here with defence production and crown assets and the defence services themselves. I am simply asking this question in an exploratory sense and now the minister has given the answer I would consequently have to go back to the Minister of National Defence to discover why he found it advisable to dispose of approximately 15,000 revolvers within the last two or three years and 400,000 rounds of cartridges.
There is just one other question along that line. The prices to the purchasers seem to be very reasonable. I take it that in the report of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation on page 20, where about ten lines from the top cartridge ball is mentioned and in brackets the figure 311,900 appears it would represent the quantity, and the price is shown as being $4,751.51, which means that these cartridges are selling for one and a half cents

apiece. I have no idea whether that is just the bid the corporation gets for this material or whether it is the price they set on it but certainly the ammunition is selling very cheaply.
It would be very interesting to know what that ammunition cost when the Department of Defence Production was producing it and it would also be interesting to know what the pistols cost which were selling in 1955 for $3.75 or $7.40. These prices must be just a fraction of the original cost of the ammunition and the revolvers.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
in selling revolvers my hon. friend will appreciate we do not sell them from door to door. We must be very sure of the disposition of the revolvers we sell, and very often they are sold with an undertaking that they will be mutilated and converted into scrap. Where we have an article that can be sold freely we must call for tenders and advertise the sale and the company accepts the highest tender. I have no way, and I am sure my hon. friend has no way, of knowing the condition of the ammunition. It may have deteriorated. I think a good deal of ammunition does come for disposal due to the fact that it is over age and therefore not serviceable for the armed services. Whether this is a part of that, I cannot say, but the rule of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation is that every sale is advertised in the newspapers and the highest bid is accepted.

There is one point on which
I would like some information and that is the operation of the mid-Canada line. What are the plan's for actually operating the line once it has been completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
the line is now being constructed and the management agency for the construction is the Trans-Canada Telephone Company. They have designated the Bell Telephone Company as the agent for the company in charge of this particular project.
The line is due to be put into operation on January 1 next. That date still seems to be valid and is the original date planned. So far as I know it will be carried out. Nevertheless the construction of the line will not be fully completed for another several months. There will be testing of equipment required arid tuning up and that sort of thing. It is the proposal of defence production with the concurrence of the services to arrange an operating contract with the Trans-Canada Telephone Company for the first three years and that contract is now being negotiated.
I think my hon. friend would agree it would be a tragedy to have one organization
Supply-Defence Production building the line and another organization operating it. You would have a gap there which I think would be dangerous for the owner and that is what we are trying to arrange for by this negotiating contract.
Does that mean in effect that the Bell Telephone Company will be operating the line?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

What companies make up
the Trans-Canada Telephone Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: B.C. Telephone Company, Alberta Government Telephones, Saskatchewan Government Telephones, Manitoba Telephone System, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, New Brunswick Telephone Company Limited and Maritime Telegraph and Telephone Company Limited. While Bell is the agency for having the work done under the contract, all these companies make a contribution to the work. For instance, if we are building a station in northern Alberta, Alberta Telephone supply the equipment and men needed in constructing and operating the line. It is expected that Bell will draw on all the companies making up the Trans-Canada telephone system. The manning is quite a problem as provision must be made for rotation. I doubt if technical men can be kept in the north for more than one year at a time and it is quite important that the company which undertakes the operation be able to rotate employees so that an employee leaving the line will not be out of a job. That is the advantage of having Trans-Canada Telephone.
Will there be any civilian use permitted of the mid-Canada line?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, it is restricted now and I think it always will be restricted to military use. The communications system must be instantly available in /case warning is given anywhere on the line and it must not be cluttered up with civilian messages or the staff supposed to be watching for military messages must not be worrying about civilian messages.
Is there more equipment being installed than is required for defence purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Just the minimum for defence purposes.
Can the minister give the approximate number of men required to man the line?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Approximately 800.

That would be entirely civilian staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I had better read the explanation here. The item is to provide for the cost of care, maintenance and custody of defence plants in standby condition and for the care and maintenance of buildings, machine tools, equipment and production tooling, including the costs of dismantling, packaging, crating, transportation, inhibiting, storage and other expenses incidental to the preservation of such facilities which may be required again. It is essential to ensure that buildings, machinery and equipment, assets which make up key defence production lines, do not deteriorate upon completion of various production contracts.
In order to do this it may be necessary, where arrangements cannot be made to continue production for defence purposes or to meet the problem by using crown owned facilities for commercial purposes on an adequate rental basis, to preserve production lines in such a manner that they can readily be put back into service with little or no delay. In most cases, capital assets which make up these key production lines are crown owned. However, there are a limited number of cases where, in order to preserve a vital production line comprised of intermingled crown owned and privately owned capital assets, it may be necessary to reimburse the private owners for keeping their assets in an inactive status.
Therefore, it is proposed to take the following action where necessary to ensure preservation of key production facilities:
(a)	Preserve fully integrated crown owned defence plants and buildings, in part or in full, in standby condition;

(b)	Move capital assistance assets and production tooling from a contractor's plant to government warehouse for storage or preservation in situ, or move to other contractor's plants when advisable. In the latter event, repairs, adaptations and moving costs would be paid from this item.
(c)	Preserve contractor owned equipment in a standby condition.

Mr. Chairman, may I say just a word in connection with estimating? On June 29, 1956, the hon. member for Eglinton questioned the accuracy of departmental estimating by comparing the moneys voted by parliament with actual expenditures made by the department. I would like to point out that most of the difference was in the capital assistance votes and that this type of vote has a number of variable factors which must be taken into account because they involve relatively large contingencies of a kind not required in most departmental votes.
A review of the figures relating to the capital assistance votes shows that a little over $300 million was voted in the last five fiscal years, and that actual expenditures accounted for slightly less than half that amount. The difference, of course, is comprised of the amounts which lapsed at the end of each fiscal year. It should not be assumed, however, that because the balances were allowed to lapse, the moneys should not have been voted in the first place.
Some 20 per cent of the total voted, or $82 million, represented moneys revoted because the projects were not completed in time to pay all the accounts from the original vote. The net amounts voted for new projects were, therefore, in the order of $220 million. It might also be observed that the largest portion of the revotes occurred during the early days of the present defence program when shortages and bottlenecks made it difficult to judge the rate at which projects would be completed. As the program continued, work on capital projects proceeded at a more uniform rate, and in the last fiscal year only 9 per cent of the total vote was for funds committed but not paid in that fiscal year.
Another explanation accounting for more than one-third of the total lapses, or 20 per


cent of the total amount voted, relates to projects not proceeded with but which were under consideration at the time the estimates were prepared, which was six months in advance of the fiscal year. You will appreciate that, in a defence production program, plans have to be made well in advance, often on the basis of projected requirements of the Department of National Defence. In some cases we were able to persuade private industry to build or acquire the necessary facilities and equipment, or we found that other arrangements could be made. In other instances, it was found after careful study of all the facts that the requirement had changed and the project was no longer needed.
Lapses occasioned by overestimating the cost of approved projects amounted to $15 million, or 5 per cent of the total voted, and this margin does not seem unreasonable.
My hon. friend says that at this stage we should have changed our views and decided that a lot less money is required. We are unable to do that. We are the servants of the Department of National Defence. If, tomorrow, the Department of National Defence tells us to close down one of our principal plants we close it down immediately. But what do we do with the equipment? We can sell the plant, perhaps. We had a case a while ago of a hexachlorethane plant that had been very active for a great many years. It ran out of orders. We had to close it down. We had to inhibit the equipment. We know the plant will be needed again whether there is war or peace, and we spent a good deal of money on that project. There may be similar cases tomorrow or the next day or another day. If we have not the money we just have to let the machinery deteriorate until we get the money.
I can assure my hon. friend that I have discussed the matter with my officers in the luncheon period and I am assured that they believe this estimate is just as valid today as it was when the estimates were first prepared. In the circumstances I cannot for a moment consider reducing the amount of the estimate.

On item 87, Mr. Chairman, I note that the vote is mainly concerned with capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors engaged in defence contracts, et cetera. There is a reduction of almost $1 million in this item for the current year and I presume this trend will be continued as we recede from the Korean war emergency.
I recall that when the Department of Defence Production was re-established to meet the Korean crisis this sum for capital assistance reached quite substantial proportions.
We in western Canada were extremely interested in this particular aspect of the Department of Defence Production and our chambers of commerce and business and industrial leaders made very strong efforts to ensure that western Canada and particularly the prairie provinces would receive an equitable share of the new upsurge in defence production.
We remembered the experience of world war II when the prairie provinces became depopulated almost overnight as our young people moved to fill the labour demands in the defence factories that were mushrooming in eastern and central Canada to meet the industrial demands of world war II.
There seem to be several hon. members who want to make speeches at this time, Mr. Chairman.

Finish your speech.
Go ahead.
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am suffering from a cold, Mr. Chairman; otherwise I could make my voice heard above the noise in the chamber.
Examining the public accounts of Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955 it would seem we have not had too much success in overcoming the mistakes that were made in the build-up of world war II so far as a more equitable distribution of defence industry across the country is concerned.
As I look at page DD-3, a list of capital assistance items totalling over $25 million, I observe that with only three exceptions out of a long list covering pages DD-3 and DD-4 each one of those capital assistance grants was made in some part of Ontario or some part of Quebec.
The same pattern is observed in the contract awards of over $25,000 outlined on page DD-4 of the public accounts. In like manner the grants in lieu of taxes for defence industries are all concentrated in the two central regions. This is a complaint that has been raised in the house from time to time particularly by members from the western and maritime provinces and I would like to frame it in a specific question at this time.
I note, for example, that the Minister of Defence Production has considerable influence in this regard because on page 26 of the report of his department, in the first paragraph under the heading "Industry and Defence", we read the following:
In addition to purchasing responsibilities, the Minister of Defence Production is charged with responsibility for organizing and mobilizing the resources of Canada, including the co-ordination of economic and industrial facilities, in order to meet the current and prospective needs of defence.
That is a big item. The minister has almost complete power and responsibility over a large segment of our economy. Continuing with the quotation:
The general economic background against which the program will have to be carried out must be taken into account in discharging these responsibilities, which fall into two main categories. The first is the development and maintenance of production capabilities (i.e. adequate facilities, skilled labour, engineering experience and technical knowledge) which are required to meet the equipment needs of the armed forces. The second is the availability of the strategic and basic materials needed to carry out the defence production program.
As I have already indicated, that gives the minister tremendous responsibility in seeing that the defence industry as it moves forward fits into the general economic scheme of things in a most effective and efficient way. I would point out that the fact we have failed to overcome the mistakes of world war II when defence industry was largely

Supply-Defence Production concentrated in the two central provinces would suggest there is a genuine cause for complaint from those of us who represent western constituencies. The economic trends have been analysed in a summary fashion by the Financial Post. In the issue of July 7 there is an analysis carried out by Mr. J. K. Edmunds who projects the economic patterns in Canada for the year 1980. That projection incidentally is based largely on the very copious evidence submitted in various briefs to the Gordon commission. On the basis of that evidence Mr. Edmunds concludes that by 1980 Canada will have a population of 28 million, 75 per cent of which will be living in towns and cities and 65 per cent in central Canada. That reinforces the assumption that as far ahead as 1980, more than two decades, the present unfortunate trends will still be continuing, producing a state of industrial and economic imbalance even at that far distant date.
I should like the minister to indicate what steps are being taken to reverse these trends as far as possible. According to the information contained in his report, obviously he has the power to do this and obviously it is in the best interests of Canada that we try to establish a more equitable pattern of national development across the country. The huge expenditures involved in the Department of Defence Production provide a most fruitful source of brighter prospects in this regard. The main estimates today seem to be along the lines of electronic and aircraft development, two items of manufacture which could easily be carried out in the relatively sparsely settled parts of the three western provinces.
One final word on this score, and I think this is my strongest argument in this regard. Last week Canada engaged in a comprehensive civil defence exercise. For three or four days headlines screamed from the papers. Of course they were mock headlines, but the whole scheme was carried out as realistically as possible. Those headlines stated that large metropolitan areas had been completely wiped out as a result of attack by guided missiles with nuclear warheads. One report I read said that the city of Montreal had been completely wiped out.
The various departments of government responsible for the defence of Canada seem to be working at cross purposes. The civil defence people are warning the public of the dire prospects in the event of attack of that kind, which we hope will never happen. We are told that large metropolitan areas like Montreal can be wiped out by one nuclear weapon strategically exploded in the right


spot. Yet it would seem from the information which I have placed before the committee and which I gleaned from various reports that we are still continuing to concentrate our strategic industries in these vulnerable urban centres.
I wonder if the minister could give us any idea as to what steps if any are being taken to disperse this concentration of industry so that we may have the necessary defence in the case of possible nuclear attack and also, more positively, that we may have in Canada a more equitable distribution of industry across the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of capital assistance is to create facilities for the production of a given war store. The governing factors in the allocation geographically are the availability of skilled labour, the availability of management capable of handling the task, the availability of power, the availability of raw materials and the availability of subcontractors if subcontractors are required. Generally speaking it does not allow too much latitude to the department as to where a plant might be located. The situation usually indicates pretty clearly where the plant should be located.
When we do have a choice we always give preference to a location outside the industrial areas of Ontario and Quebec. For instance, we have given a good deal of capital assistance in the maritime provinces when perhaps we could have done equally well or better in the central provinces. We have put a fair amount of capital assistance into the west, particularly on the west coast, with a fair amount in Winnipeg. But in those cases we were dealing with the type of product which was suitable to the labour n the area. The production was such as could be obtained without too large a shift in population. Obviously if you must build a new plant and housing to house employees, if you must bring in your skilled management and skilled labour, you have a very expensive type of production.
We are simply the agents for the armed forces and are using their funds. We must be able to assure them that we are doing that economically. Within these narrow limits we do attempt to diversify the location of our capital assisted projects but, as I said previously, we have very little latitude in that regard. I am inclined to think that within the discretion available to us we have done a pretty fair job.
The item we have before us deals almost wholly with aircraft and is almost wholly

devoted to the CF-105 program. The details of the program are as follows:
Aircraft	 $6,906,570
Ammunition	 740,000
Electronics	 750,000
Guns	 5,500
Sundries	 40,817
From that we deduct $1,443,683 which represents cash not required during the fiscal year 1956-57. Obviously the only place you can spend money being used to advance the CF-105 program is in the vicinity of the Avro plant at Toronto. I do not know how we can exercise much latitude for the benefit of the city of Brandon or any other point in the west.

I want to thank the minister for his comments on this important subject. I noticed he raised the matter of the availability of technical skill and labour. I want to assure him that in any part of western Canada we have all sorts of potential labour, labour that is obviously quite mobile judging from the fact that a good many of the workers in the defence plants of Ontario and Quebec originally came from the prairies. A couple of weeks ago it was my privilege to attend the 75th anniversary celebration of the community of Boissevain, Manitoba, in the heart of perhaps the richest agricultural area in the west.
Go easy now.

Well, even taking into
account the constituency of the hon. member for Selkirk I think I can say that it is the richest agricultural area-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In southwestern Manitoba.

Yes. They published a very interesting book, "The Beckoning Hills", which reviews the history of that community from its origin in 1881 down to the present time. It is full of all sorts of anecdotes concerning the pioneering spirit of the people who settled that part of Canada so recently, because after all 75 years is a fairly recent period of time in the whole span of man's history. It is hardly more than the biblical span of a man's lifetime. The book gives the population statistics and they indicate the problem that the prairie provinces as a whole are up against.
In 1901, 20 years after the first settlement, the population of this part of the country was 6,430. By 1926 it had increased to 7,011. In 1931 it was 7,340 and in 1941 it was 6,478. There had been an exodus of almost a thousand people from this rich agricultural area under the first impact of the war. The downward trend increased up to 1946, and the census of 1951 gave the total population of that area as 5,615, or almost a thousand less
Supply-Defence Production than there were in 1901. That is what you call making progress going backwards. The difficulty arises, of course, because of the changing conditions of agriculture, mechanization and so forth, which are causing widespread depopulation of the prairies.
I realize that the item we are dealing with at the moment does not cover comprehensively the problem I am concerned with, and I must admit there have been some excellent and worth-while developments to meet this problem in the city of Winnipeg. I believe, for example, that a component of the CF-100 is being produced by the Bristol Corporation in Winnipeg, which is a step in the right direction, and I presume that the same trend will follow as we move into the production of the CF-105.
I re-emphasize this problem repeatedly because I think such assistance is one of the most fruitful ways of dealing with the basic economic problem confronting Canada at the present time, namely, more and more concentration in a relatively small area of Canada. I was particularly shocked to see that a projection of our economy to 1980 in that very reliable source, the Financial Post, indicates that this concentration will go on as a continuous trend.
By way of further detailed information, has the minister information available indicating what capital assistance programs have been established? Can he give some specific examples of capital programs that have gone forward in the prairie region as part of the activities of the Department of Defence Production since the beginning of the Korean crisis?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I might point out to my hon. friend that he overlooks one factor. A plant to produce war material must be a big plant. In other words, you do not make war material by the piece; you make it by volume.
You do with aeroplanes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Where do you have small plants? Just name me a small plant that makes aeroplanes.
Component parts.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Component parts, certainly. We do not usually have to give capital assistance to get component parts made. We use existing plants. But may I point this out to my hon. friend? Suppose we went to Boissevain and put up a plant there that required 5,000 people or 500 people, if you like. You would dislocate that area for years. I remember well when General Motors went to Regina in the late twenties and established a plant there. I think they went

Supply-Defence Production there about 1926 and in 1932 they closed the plant down after having moved 1,000 or 1,200 people out there. That gave Regina a set-back from which it did not recover for ten years. That would be exactly the position in Boissevain if you put a war plant there.
One thing we must watch is to see that you do not create that kind of dislocation. If you put up a war plant it should be in an area where it can be converted to civilian production and have a chance of surviving as a privately owned plant. The hon. member asks what western plants we have helped. We have helped Bristol Engines with considerable capital assistance, also Standard Aero Engine of Winnipeg, Northwest Industries of Edmonton and I think one or two plants in Calgary. But to obtain the size of production that we require for war we must go into areas that can furnish the manpower and the skilled supervision without a great dislocation of population.
In the maritimes we have put a good deal of capital assistance into New Glasgow, a fair amount into Amherst, a fair amount into Saint John in the shipbuilding industry there, and a very considerable amount in Halifax. Where we have had populations and locations suitable for the kind of work we have wanted to do we have spread the work around as much as we could.

I agree that the establishment of the parts assembly plant at Regina came at a very unfortunate time in the predepression era, and I think the dislocation that occurred in Regina and throughout all the prairie provinces for that matter during that unfortunate period was brought about by more than the necessity of closing the parts assembly plant at Regina. I further agree that you would not expect to establish a plant employing 5,000 people in a community the size of Boissevain. It would have a tremendous impact on the community in all respects which perhaps could not be absorbed by the social amenities that exist there already. That is not exactly what I am thinking about.
Having mentioned Boissevain, may I say there is one industry there, a private endeavour, making laminated structures. It was established in the past few years and it employs some 40 or 50 men. It is making quite a contribution to the vitality of that particular community. It is handicapped by the freight rate problem. The Canadian Railways do not allow in transit rate privileges as the railways of the United States do in an attempt to assist the establishment of industry in their prairie region.
I should like to say further, Mr. Chairman, that private industry generally is ahead of


the government in recognizing the changed circumstances on the prairies. We now have a sufficiently large population-following the population recession of the war we are now beginning to move forward-to provide a fairly strong local demand. Particularly in the field of the manufacture of electrical parts we have a shift from the east to western Canada and also in the packaging and manufacturing of food products. For example, the Campbell Soup Company is contemplating establishing a further branch plant in Manitoba. The emphasis that I should like to see maintained is the emphasis that the department itself was trying to maintain. When the defence production activity got under way, within the department there was established a small defence industries branch which functioned for three years and then disappeared. When I queried the minister on that point, he said that it had carried out its role adequately and that it had done the necessary job. I did not agree with that statement at the time and I still do not agree with it. I thought that was an excellent innovation in these complex affairs, namely making certain that every possible provision was being made to decentralize this huge accumulation of defence industries which have become established largely around the two urban centres, namely Toronto and Montreal and which overnight would be destroyed-the whole defence industrial potential would be destroyed-if we ever faced an atomic attack. I suggest that we might well keep in mind the objective that was indicated in connection with the small defence production branch in trying to establish the manufacture of component parts of various electronic equipment for aircraft on as widely-scattered or as widely-dispersed a basis as possible.

Before this item carries I should like to follow along on the thoughts that have been expressed by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and the review that has been given by the Minister of Defence Production. I appreciate the fact that this item is a centralizing one but it is an item that needs generally a great deal of consideration and future planning. The minister referred to the fact that Saint John and Halifax are getting some assistance in connection with their shipyards. That is true, but I would say that it is a very small amount of assistance compared with what the shipyards on the St. Lawrence are getting. Two or three years ago in the town of Marysville in New Brunswick we had an example of a textile industry closing down. At that time something was said-and I think some approaches were made-with respect to the possibility of

locating there some sort of government-assisted industry to replace this textile factory that it was necessary to close. I do not know whether or not it would have been possible to do something there, but certainly the facilities were available, namely a factory in fairly good shape, some labour and some market.
If we take the attitude that has been suggested, namely that we can locate only where there are available population, labour and materials, I suppose we shall never be able to disperse industry in any way. In New Brunswick also a short time ago we had an example in connection with the army camp work there. I do not want to go into the details of the contracts, because the matter has been mentioned here before. I just want to say that there was a problem in connection with the letting of those large contracts by the Department of Defence Production in connection with the camp. The department naturally wanted to get the work done as cheaply as possible and in as modern a way as possible. In most cases they call for tenders in connection with large contracts. I suppose that is the businesslike way to do the thing. But our smaller contractors were not able to get together and were not able to extend themselves for these larger jobs.
I put this reservation in these remarks, Mr. Chairman. We have had some contracts and since the initial planning others have been given. I mention the matter only in order to say that the problem is there, and it is the same one that is there with respect to this other work. The United States have had this difficulty to contend with for many years and they have taken many measures to overcome it. They have set up entire new communities for their large plants. I remember reading that in the New England states a method was found whereby the federal government could give some type of depreciation assistance to an industry in a certain locality. In that way the burden and the initial difficulty with respect to an industry surviving or even locating in a tough area would fall on the federal authorities rather than on the local municipal people who were already burdened, as has already been mentioned in recent debates. I appreciate the difficulties and I have mentioned these examples merely to show that it is a problem that is becoming of increasing importance. In the United States, in England and in Scotland they have had to do something about it. I suggest to the minister that we must have some careful planning for the future. In his department he has experts. Probably they could look into the matter. If this amount needs to be extended or to have its scope broadened, I am sure that the areas in the
Supply-Defence Production prairies and in the maritimes would greatly benefit. Such a procedure would get over some of the criticism that we have heard in recent days with respect to the difficulties there.

Mr. Chairman, the debate so far has brought to my mind a few remarks that I should like to make at this time. We have been talking about decentralization of war plants, labour and so on. I should like to refer the minister to the Canadian Arsenals plant at Lindsay, Ontario, which has had three quite definite lay-offs since last year. Employment there is getting fairly small. I should like the minister and his officials to give consideration to that plant. With their large budget I do not see why they cannot create some employment in the town of Lindsay.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I may say to my hon. friend that we have been looking at that situation very hard. We hope to get some work for it. The Lindsay plant is more or less a specialty shop. It does small runs of ammunition because of the nature of its equipment. We try to bring them along regularly, but I know it has hit a little low spot recently. We hope we can improve the situation.

I wish to draw attention to the fact that in Campbellton we have the McLennan Engineering Works. Some years ago this firm spent a considerable amount of money becoming equipped to repair aircraft engines. The contracts that they obtained from the government lasted a very short time, and afterwards they were denied any further work. In the last two years McLennan Engineering Works have not had any federal work and this tremendous investment which they were encouraged by the federal government to make is now going to waste. I would recommend that the minister check into the amount of repair work we have received in the maritimes. We have several plants fully equipped to do federal work, such as the McLennan Engineering Works, but for the past three or four years they have not been favoured with any work. This places a terrific burden, not only on the owners of the plants but on the public and on the employees who are dependent on these plants to make a livelihood. I am sure the minister will be kind enough to look into this matter and do something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will be glad to look into it.

I should like to point out that last year the department asked for and obtained a vote of $8,250,000 for this item. The minister reported yesterday that the

Supply-Defence Production department actually expended during the last fiscal year $2,084,615 on this item. It is quite clear, therefore, that the amount that was voted that was proven not to be necessary was over $6,150,000. In other words, the amount actually required, as shown by experience as reflected in the actual expenditures, was only a small fraction of the total estimate. It was just about 25 per cent of the amount the department asked parliament to vote.
The minister was frank enough to say that this item of capital assistance is one with which the department has had most difficulty in estimating over the years. I drew attention on June 29 to the fact that for this item in the fiscal year 1951-52, parliament was asked to vote and did vote $100 million for this purpose, whereas the sum expended was $22,190,419. Perhaps I could just give the amounts in round figures, Mr. Chairman. The following year, 1952-53, parliament voted $110 million and the sum expended was $78 million. In the fiscal year 1953-54, the sum asked for by the department and voted was $60 million. The sum expended by the department was $36 million. In the fiscal year 1954-55, the sum asked for by the department, and voted by parliament, was $25 million, and the sum expended was $7 million. Now, we have before us the experience of the fiscal year 1955-56 and we see that although the department asked for $8,250,000, and parliament voted that sum, the actual need was only one-quarter of that sum.
So, Mr. Chairman, for the same reasons that I put before the committee in connection with the last item, I think it is our responsibility here to make sure that the estimates that we approve and pass are closely in line with the proven requirements of the department, and I move:
That item 87 be reduced by the sum of $5 million to $2,500,000.
I point out, Mr. Chairman, that that amendment would leave the department with a substantial sum of money more than it actually found necessary last year. Last year it found it necessary to expend $2,084,615, and this amendment would provide them with $2,500,000, a figure almost 20 per cent larger than their actual expenditures for the fiscal year which ended March 31, 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I may say that if this motion passes it will set the CF-105 program back at least 12 months. We are already committed for considerably more money than would be left in this vote if this amendment passed.
For how much are you committed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We have to build certain test facilities for a supersonic engine which is being developed there, and we must provide certain new equipment for the aircraft plant. We have already approved expenditures and commitments, but we would have to withdraw the commitment. I know all these commitments depend on parliament voting the money, but that is the particular situation in this case.
I am surprised, really, at being criticized for not spending all the capital assistance for which we asked parliament. We know what we have to have, roughly, in the next year, but we do not know the extent to which we may be able to persuade private industry to put up the capital themselves. We do our best. We part with capital assistance money very reluctantly and I may say it has been practically cut off at the present time except for the aircraft industry where we are bringing out a new plane and where new techniques, new testing equipment and new facilities are required. As I say, we are committed, not for the full amount, but we are committed for over half of it. If this vote passes, I will just write A. V. Roe that they will have to do without for another 12 months. They will have to do the best they can after that.
What is the precise amount of your commitment to A. V. Roe?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is around $5 million. We cannot say exactly because we do not know exactly what these things will cost. We have authorized certain work to be done under capital assistance. It is somewhere between $4-5 million and $5 million. We know other work must be carried out. What we do not know is whether we can persuade private industry to furnish additional facilities that we must have. If we cannot do that, we must put up the money as capital assistance. It is as simple as that. Go ahead and vote on your amendment, if you want to. I am tempted not to vote on this amendment and let it go through and let the opposition take the responsibility for it. I think that is about what the hon. member for Eglinton is asking for, and should get it.
That was a silly, stupid, concluding remark, Mr. Chairman. This is the first time the minister has spoken about the CF-105 production program being attached to this item.

Mr. Chairman, I will just start to say a few words in English in order to tell the minister where I am leading. About two weeks ago I asked a question regarding the sale of the Riviere du Loup arsenal, and in reply to my question I received an answer on July 23. The first question was as follows:
1.	Have the Riviere du Loup arsenal buildings been sold? If so, on what date?
The answer was:
1.	Yes. Agreement of sale executed following order in council of May 24, 1956. Possession of property given purchaser on June 29, 1956.
The second question was:
2.	What was the amount of the sale and what were the conditions of payment?
The answer was:
2.	Sale was made after public advertisement of the property for $17,500 cash.
The third question was as follows:
3.	What was the conversion cost of the former Canadian National shops, which subsequently became the Riviere du Loup arsenal?
Listen to the answer:
3.	The Canadian National Railways shops at Riviere du Loup were transferred to Canadian Arsenals Limited and converted for the production of components for -50'' and 20 mm ammunition at a cost of $285,453.80 to meet orders valued at $3,835,000.
(Translation) ;
Mr. Chairman, it is now definitely established that the Riviere du Loup arsenal, which operated for three years only, was sold by tender for $17,500, whereas an amount of $285,453.80 had been spent in order to convert the former Canadian National plants into an arsenal. Even if it served to produce about $4 million worth of small arms ammunition, this arsenal operated for only three years, during which employment was available to a very limited number of people. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that instead of going to this fabulous expense, it would have been possible in view of the few people employed there, to have the same done at Quebec or Valcartier arsenal, thus avoiding considerable lay-offs.
I return now to the price paid for this building and the property on which it is built. It is an excellent building, with magnificent grounds, and yet they were sold for the ridiculous sum of $17,500, whereas the department had formerly spent on the rehabilitation of the same premises the considerable amount of nearly $300,000. Therefore
Supply-Defence Production the transaction involved only about six per cent of the original amount. In other words, the loss involved was exactly 94 cents out of every dollar. This, I am told, was done to satisfy a company which will eventually start producing underwear in this plant.
From all this it appears that the company which has bought this arsenal is called the C. Turnbull Company Limited. If my memory serves me well, its head office is in Galt, Ontario. The surprising thing about all this though, is that until January 11, this company had held a federal charter granted on December 17, 1930, a charter which it renounced on the date I have just indicated, that is five months before purchasing the arsenal. I can say however that this company-against which I have nothing, since I do not know it, though I do know that its product is, by all accounts, excellent-has a provincial charter granted by the Ontario government. According to arrangements entered into between the provinces, it is allowed to operate in the province of Quebec, provided it abides by the laws of that province and pays corporation income tax.
The fact is, however, Mr. Chairman, that we have here a difference that is rather hard to explain. I was informed this morning that only one tender had been submitted to the department, and that was the one from the Turnbull company.
Well, you can hardly make them up.

I did not attempt to make anyone up, and I would not advise the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) to make anything up, for it would be a substantial waste of my time. I am now dealing with a serious matter, and I hope that the hon. member will stop his trifling, so that I may proceed.
It is still better than in Quebec, because, over there, no tenders are called at all.
If my hon. friend is interested in a seat in the Quebec legislature, all he has to do is to resign; but then he might have the same fate as his son.
I prefer the atmosphere of honesty in this house than that of Quebec.
Abolish Bill 34, and we will go to Quebec.

If the hon. member wants to talk of honesty, he would be well advised to wait for a judgment to be rendered shortly.

Supply-Defence Production Mr. Dupuis: If it is rendered by a man like you, I won't answer for anything.
People who live in glass houses-

He asked for it.
As I was saying, the least that this transaction suggests is objectionable favouritism. If the intention was to sell the property, conversion costs of which had amounted to close to $300,000, it seems to me that a basic price might have been set and, in this way, a more appropriate price might have been obtained.
What a businessman.

I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that such a policy is bad enough to give rise to the indignation and vigorous protests of all those who, through the taxes they pay, contribute to maintain in power a government so wasteful of the Canadian taxpayers' dollar.
Surely, the small industry which is being set up in place of the arsenal will hardly be enough to improve economic conditions in Riviere du Loup, because I am convinced that few people will find jobs in that plant. So, Mr. Chairman, it has been a waste of public moneys. We have, in the past, seen a mass exodus of Canadian National Railways' employees, especially in Riviere du Loup, who had to move to Montreal, Moncton, Campbellton and Halifax in 1952.
To Quebec.

And now, we have to stand by and see public moneys being thrown down the river, always in connection with the same building. The only conclusion is, I think, that Riviere du Loup, despite what we heard last fall, especially in September, will never be the Garden of Eden of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to mention another matter regarding the Quebec arsenal. We have in Quebec city an arsenal located below Palais hill on quite a large piece of land. I am glad that we have that plant in Quebec city for it provides work for quite a number of conscientious employees who can thus earn a decent living.
Next to that plant of Canadian Arsenals Limited, there is a nice and vast piece of land commonly called Artillery park on which stands the residence ot the superintendent of that company, a very distinguished gentleman and a great soldier, Brigadier Theriault. I say these nice things about Brigadier 

Theriault so that my hon. friends opposite will not be able to claim what they claimed the other day when speaking about the 22nd Regiment. I say that all French Canadians, and especially those in the province of Quebec, hold in high esteem and respect this distinguished soldier, Brigadier Theriault.
However, I believe that piece of land could be put to much better use than to provide luxurious accommodation for an official who certainly does not need all of it. Part of that land is wasted.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the minister sell part of that land to the city of Quebec which, I think, would be happy to buy it for several reasons, one of which would be the broadening of McMahon street, which is very narrow. It would ease traffic in that part of Quebec city and would permit the occasional parking of some 500 cars. It would also bring much more business to that business section of the city, especially for those who operate a business on Saint Jean street.
I don't ask that Brigadier Theriault be deprived of all the ground he now occupies. However, I would suggest that officials of the Department of Defence Production enter into negotiations with the city of Quebec, which is badly pressed for parking space, or try to interest certain individuals in buying that part of the property. This would help develop that important district of the city of Quebec.
It's goat's pasture.

Mr. Chairman, such was the suggestion I wanted to make in connection with that site, and I think that in so doing I have conveyed the feelings of the majority of my fellow citizens of the city of Quebec, and I trust that the department will take into serious consideration the suggestions I just made.
