Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend will grant me the indulgence of replying in English. I could try to do otherwise, but perhaps I had better not. The explanation with regard to the plant at Riviere du Loup is simple. The Canadian National Railways had a problem on their hands through the dieselization of the region, and the president informed us that the locomotive and car repair shops at Riviere du Loup were surplus to his requirements. There were about 125 families dependent

upon the work provided by those shops. He asked if we could help him out, and told us that if we could he would be pleased to deed over the property to the dominion government. Subsequently we found that we had an order for small arms ammunition amounting to about $3,800,000 which could not be handled at the Palace Hill arsenal but which could be handled at Riviere du Loup if there were some adaptation of the facilities there.
Arrangements were made accordingly. Early in 1953 the property was transferred without cost to the Department of Defence Production. Alterations were made amounting, if I remember right, to around $250,000 to provide for new facilities and installation of machinery that was moved down there from the arsenal at Quebec. For about three years we operated the plant at Riviere du Loup. In that time we turned out ammunition to the value of a little over $3 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, $3,800,000. The production was increased over what would have been possible had we operated the facilities at Quebec to full capacity. The need was there and the property at Riviere du Loup filled it very nicely.
Would the minister excuse me? I think I just heard him say that the arsenal at Quebec was working at full capacity at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
I think the minister is wrong, because it was last year and two years ago that we had so many lay-offs at Quebec and Valcartier.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
But they were mostly in the shell filling division and not in this particular division. However, we expected when we took over the property that there would be follow-up orders for small arms ammunition and these did not come. Therefore when the work was completed we were in exactly the same position as Canadian National Railways had been three years earlier. We had been employing a peak of 140 employees on the property with an average of about 105, and we faced the same serious problem of laying off these employees in an area that was not able to absorb them easily.
After discussing the matter with the mayor of Riviere du Loup we decided to call for tenders for the property with the reservation that we would not sell the property to anyone
Supply-Defence Production who could not give a reasonable guarantee of employment on about the scale we had provided in operationg it as an arsenal. Tenders were invited. We advertised in several papers. We only received one tender, and it was from a textile firm that was able to undertake to provide employment for in excess of 100 people.
The mayor favoured acceptance of the tender. True, it was a low tender; nevertheless it relieved us of the problem of maintaining a plant in idleness, which is costly; and in view of the employment situation it seemed that the right thing to do was to accept the tender, which we did. I feel that we acted as a useful link between the railway who built the plant and owned it for many years and the textile company, which is moving in at the present time. We did provide employment without any loss to the government. You can say that we spent $250,000, or whatever the figure was, in setting up the plant to make small arms ammunition. That is true, but we produced $3,800,000 worth of products; and as I remember it the margin on the product, which was for the United States government, was about 10 per cent. Therefore the story probably is that we worked there and got out without any loss of public funds. As far as Palace Hill is concerned, my hon. friend wants us to tear down a building there-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -that is older than I am. Palace Hill, from the earliest days of Quebec, has had on this site the residence of the superintendent of the arsenals.

If the minister will allow me, I never mentioned anything about destroying the Palace Hill arsenal. I am not even speaking about taking away the residence occupied now by the superintendent, Brigadier Theriault. I was just asking if the minister would not mind taking under consideration the fact that adjacent to this private residence there is a very big piece of land, a part of which the city of Quebec would be interested in buying, first of all to widen McMahon street and, second, to make a good parking area for the commercial district of Saint-Jean street.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As far as I know there has been no request to the department for that land. It is maintained by Brigadier Theriault as a public park, and it is a very beautiful park in the heart of Quebec. While we certainly would entertain a request from the city of Quebec for land sufficient to widen a street I would be very reluctant, and I think the city of Quebec would be, too,

Supply-Defence Production to do anything that would transform a beautiful park in the centre of the city into a parking space for automobiles.

First of all I wish to thank the minister for the detailed information he has given me regarding the Riviere du Loup arsenal. Can the minister tell me what the department paid for the land and buildings formerly owned by the C.N.R. which afterwards became the Riviere du Loup arsenal?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I thought I told the hon. member that the land and buildings were deeded to us without cost. They cost nothing.

May I add one word. Could it have been possible to establish a floor price before asking for the tenders to which the minister referred? I know the minister will admit, as will every hon. member of the house, that even if the plant is to employ 100 or more employees in the new operation, which I am very glad to hear, the price for which the Riviere du Loup arsenal was sold was a little bit ridiculous when we think that we had to spend $285,453.80 to convert one building and could not get a better price three years later than $17,500. I think a lot of people are worrying about the matter and are asking how this kind of transaction could take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
According to the report I received from Canadian Arsenals, if we had held the property it would have cost about $50,000 a year to keep the plant closed, maintain a watchman service and pay the taxes. To do so would also put 105 people out of work in an area where no alternative work was provided. The property was developed to repair locomotives and freight cars. Private individuals do not repair locomotives and freight cars. We took over the plant to make munitions of war. Private individuals do not make munitions of war.
The next question is, who can make use of that property? It is not everyone's meat. The fact that it is a fine plant which cost a lot of money many years ago, and cost some money for alterations and installing equipment to make munitions more recently, is interesting but it is not interesting to a man who can use the plant in Riviere du Loup and use it profitably.
We advertised for tenders. We let it be known through all our contacts that the plant was available for sale. We advertised in the papers and we got one tender. It did not take us long to decide that if we could solve the government's problem, relieve ourselves of caretaker responsibilities which might go on indefinitely, and remove ourselves from

Riviere du Loup in a way acceptable to the local people it was a very advantageous transaction as far as the Department of Defence Production was concerned.

The minister says that
advertisements were published in the papers. Can the minister say in what papers advertisements were published? Was it in the local papers or in papers throughout Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

There might be a chance that the company saw it there. But even so I find it very strange that this company in Ontario would have a chance to read this article or this advertisement in the Montreal paper. I think someone must have given this company some information of some kind.

Mr. Chairman, I approve the sale of this particular crown corporation. I approve it in the first place because I think it is good for the community. There are going to be a good many more people employed there than are employed at the present time. But I approve it mainly because of the principle involved. Today we have approximately 30 crown corporations in this country. Some of them have cost us a great deal of money. Many are being subsidized fairly extensively. I think it is a good thing for the government to get out of many of these businesses which were set up in the war period or in the emergency shortly after the war. I hope sales of this nature will happen time and time again in the near future. I should like to see other crown corporations sold also, because I think the business of government is to govern, not to be in business. From what I have seen of crown corporations in business they simply

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The estimates of this department were before the estimates committee of the House of Commons for several weeks. At that time there was a fairly complete discussion on all the items, especially on the other item under the Department of National Health and Welfare, namely civil defence, which I think was considered by the committee in sittings which extended to 10 or 12 hours. The same remark might apply to another matter that was brought up and talked about in that committee, namely the question of health insurance or hospital insurance and the proposals and discussions between the federal government and the provinces.
But in the general consideration of the estimates before the house there is no doubt that there are matters of interest which other members who were not on the estimates committee might like to discuss at this time when the estimates are before the committee of the whole. Furthermore, they may desire to obtain information that was not available to them at the time the estimates committee was sitting or because they were unable to attend. They might desire of their own accord to discuss some of these matters with the minister.
It has always been my belief that the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, dealing as they do with matters which are so important to the well-being and happiness of the people of the country, should receive fuller consideration by the house than they do receive, and that more time than is usually spent on them should be devoted to their consideration. I think the fact that the estimates of this department were sent to a committee this year was an excellent thing. As a result of questioning the minister and his officials I believe more information was obtained in that committee than would have been obtained as the result of a few hours' discussion in this chamber. Of course every person did not agree in that
64S6

Supply-Health and Welfare committee, but there was that opportunity-available and there was the fullest discussion of these matters.
In so far as the estimates of this department are concerned, there should be unanimous agreement throughout the committee today that the matter of keeping well is of the utmost importance to the people of this country. But if you go back a few hundred years in European history you will find that the point of view among those who were interested in the healing arts was concerned with the curing of disease. There is a great deal of difference between using preventive measures and curing. The idea of preventive measures probably never crossed their minds at that time. The most they could hope for was to have physicians who were sufficiently versed in an understanding of disease that sick people under their care would rapidly get well.
Under these conditions it is clear that only a small proportion of the population could share in the benefits of the increasing skill of these physicians. But today hospitals, laboratories and physicians are in close contact with new scientific equipment. They are armed with new drugs and they are providing a medical service today that would have been unbelievable in the eighteenth century. Even today improving our methods of curing disease is not sufficient, and I emphasize the word "curing", the problem today is to get people well and to keep them well. This is the prime objective of the people who are working in the fields of public health and preventive medicine.
Throughout the last decade especially great progress has been made in the curing and treatment of disease. There are, however, still many problems, and there is a demand for still more rapid progress. But if we look back over the last 20 years on the discoveries that have been made in that time, we can see that there is every reason to believe that it will come. Equally new and exciting results will follow the new and exciting discoveries which have been made. But if we still pursued the old idea of keeping people well by curing disease, it would involve a tremendous expenditure on the part of the nation. From the standpoint of the taxpayer it would be a very expensive proposition. It would require the training of a large number of professional people to keep all the people cured of disease.
Today we have developed a public health program to such an extent, and this is coupled with our increasing knowledge of preventive medicine, that we are making remarkable progress in the campaign to keep people well. As the program advances the costs of keeping people well will decrease.


At the present time one could visualize that the future may bring a period when the need for hospitals will diminish, so that the health program in continuing to keep people well will become the great objective rather than the older concept of curing disease.
I came across a quotation from a very eminent man, Dr. C. E. Winslow, a very distinguished man in the field of public health. This was written in 1949 but I think it still applies today. The quotation is as follows:
As I see it today, public health is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting physical and mental health and efficiency through organized community efforts for the sanitation of the environment, the control of community infections, the education of the individual in the principles of personal hygiene, the organization of medical and nursing service for the early diagnosis and treatment of disease, and the development of the social machinery which will ensure to every individual in the community a standard of living adequate for the maintenance of health.
This statement, made by such an eminent man, applies today with greater force than it did seven years ago. I think he has covered the whole field in that one short statement.
Now, in so far as present conditions in Canada are concerned, I am not going to attempt to cover all the diseases and all the troubles with which medical men in Canada are faced today. There are two or three that I intend to discuss for a short time before this committee. I shall first consider the question of cancer. Statistics show that this is still the great scourge. It is true that there have been marked advances in the treatment of this disease in the primary type. The difficulty there lies in getting these patients at the time the disease first makes its appearance, in the primary lesion stage. Then a great deal more could be done in a curative way in protecting these people. Possibly more advanced diagnostic methods have shown a larger number of the population to be suffering from the disease; nevertheless a high percentage still appears in our mortality rates.
In that regard, X-ray facilities along with other means of diagnosis have shown that many of those people who possibly were undiagnosed at previous times are now getting a more complete diagnosis, and this accounts for some of the rise in the death rate attributed to cancer. But it is also true of this disease, as it is true of heart disease and the group of people who suffer from cardiovascular disease-that is disease of the heart and blood vessels-that as the span of life has been lengthened we seem to have more people suffering from this disease than we

formerly did. Not only that, sir, but in so far as the mortality rates are concerned we are going to have older people ultimately succumbing to this disease.
So I have one plea and one suggestion to the minister today in regard to cancer, and it is this. While research is costly, no apparently worth-while project in research looking toward the discovery of the cause of cancer, or even of the treatment, should be neglected through lack of funds. While other nations are spending funds in the common objective of the solution of this scourge, I believe our Canadian scientists are capable of contributing a great deal toward scientific research. They are capable of contributing a share, as they have shown in the past, that will compare favourably with that of any nation in the world.
This is a disease that has baffled all the greatest workers in the world in the scientific field. But the big problem today under present conditions, knowing as we do very little though advances have been made regarding the cause of cancer, is to intensify the measures that have already been taken to hold the disease in check. The other big problem is getting the people to go to the physician or to report to a treatment centre when the very earliest symptoms come upon them. Then more can be done toward cutting down the mortality resulting from cancer.
The other subject I shall discuss today, sir, is mental disease. Unfortunately in Canada there has been a very definite rise in the percentage of cases of this disease. Tuberculosis is now under control. There was a time when we spent a great deal of time in this house discussing tuberculosis. I may say that due to the advent of new methods of treatment and scientific measures, especially in the field of public health, this disease has been brought well under control. Our campaign now is to try to find these isolated cases, keep checking up on them, and eliminate the disease for all time.
In that regard, a great deal of work is being done in my own province-I am not conversant with the work in the other provinces'-in mass surveys. If 4,000 people in a town appear for X-ray and possibly three, four or five cases of incipient tuberculosis are found, even if that small proportion of the population is found suffering from this disease it makes the survey worthwhile because every one of those people is a carrier of the disease in so far as the rest of the population is concerned.
However, I was speaking of mental disease, and it continues to account for a high percentage of bed occupancy in hospitals. The provinces are spending large sums of money
Supply-Health and Welfare to provide accommodation for those who are afflicted. It is unfortunate that mental diseases for so long have produced so much suffering in the world. They have not, in general, received the same attention in the field of preventive medicine. In looking back over the history of mental disease one finds there was a time when this disease, through ignorance of the cause, was attributed to demons. Later there was a form of what might be called custodial care. The patients were shut up and their treatment was not what perhaps, in the light of present day standards, we would consider as anything less than cruel.
There may be varying causes for this increase in mental disease in Canada. Some place, somewhere, we must look for that cause and if there is a possibility of correcting it we should turn our attention to those corrective measures. We hear all sorts of reasons advanced as to why this is occurring. It may be the stress and strain of present day life. It may be that something is wrong with family relationships, or it might even be attributed to an increase in alcoholism. There is a cause for it some place. Statistics show there is a high percentage of bed occupancy in the hospitals of the country due to this disease. In fact there are as many people with mental disease occupying beds as there are with all the other bed-occupancy causes put together; that is, those who are suffering from acute diseases. The building of more hospitals will not entirely solve this problem. We also have to give up one other concept and that is the old concept of custodial care.
As far as mental disease cases are concerned, while the admission rate into hospitals does not compare with the rate for those who are admitted for medicine and surgery, it is the slowness of the recovery of those people that is a major cause of the hospitalization. But there is one bright spot, Mr. Chairman, and that is the number of cases that are being discharged as cured from those institutions. In view of that fact, I think we have made a great deal of progress along the line of dealing with the disease. The only thing now is to do something further. If we can correct the cause of this disease, if we can by treatment or prevention do something toward eliminating a great deal of this trouble that is afflicting people, then we shall be making quite a bit of progress.
If we take mental disease as an example, history has shown that interest in the treatment of the disease has always preceded interest in its prevention. Success has now been shown in the treatment and the outlook is brighter. As I said before, that brighter outlook can be seen from the large number

Supply-Health and Welfare of discharges of people after short-term treatment, and of people who were afflicted for longer periods.
What we require in dealing with this disease that seems to be uppermost in the concern of those who are working in the field of public health is hospitalization, of course, where it is required, and mental hygiene clinics and more trained personnel. If we are to carry on a successful campaign against the incidence of this disease we require more people who are trained both in the treatment and the nursing of this disease.
There is one other point I should like to make. I made an appeal to the minister concerning the question of coronary disease. When the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs were up I suggested to the minister that a study could be made of that older group among the returned veterans, especially of world war I and of world war II. I suggested that they could go through their hospital records and thereby derive certain information regarding the cause of coronary disease. If there is one group of people who were subjected to the strains and stresses it is the veterans of the first and second world wars.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs agreed to consider it. I suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this is one group with respect to which he could lend assistance in a study of the causes of this disease. This disease is becoming pretty common. You can hardly pick up a newspaper nowadays without noticing that some well-known man, possibly a man who had a great deal to contribute toward the building up of this country, has suddenly passed out from this disease. It is not just a disease of old age that is afflicting people who have a great deal to contribute. It is afflicting people at the age of 40, 45 or 50. You see very promising careers cut off suddenly by this disease. It is true that a fair number of them recover, but on the other hand they have to live within their limitations and possibly are not as active as they would have been if they had not suffered from the disease.
Unfortunately the whole picture in regard to the percentage of mortality cases is changing; coronary disease, listed of course with diseases of the heart, is coming up to the top of the list. If anything should be done it is research, research into the diet and into the way in which people live. There is a cause for this increase in the number of these cases. It is gratifying to know that last year an organization made its first appearance in Ottawa. It was a group of specialists


formed to consider this disease. There is a great field for them in this work. I was certainly glad to see that a beginning had been made among a body of men who are so well acquainted with the disease. I think it will do a great deal to stimulate research into the question, and it certainly should be to the advantage of the citizens of this country.
Another thing that seems to be bothering the health authorities is the incidence of cardio-vascular disease among our people. We commonly call it high blood pressure. Further study should be made of this disease and information should be derived from that research which would produce new procedures for the early detection of heart disease, and facilitate treatment and improve further the prognosis.
There are many subjects, sir, that should receive consideration by this committee. I have spoken of these two, mental disease and coronary disease, because of their increasing incidence. However, I wish to refer briefly to the importance of the benefits of research grants and fellowship programs. I know that a great deal has been done in this country, but I feel that the more research we can afford, the more money that is devoted to research by the department, the more will be done in that regard and it will pay for itself in time in relieving suffering and in cutting down the incidence of disease.
There are many fields in medicine which are left to be explored, so that any country such as ours needs an adequate force of skilled scientists and more information if we are to solve such health problems as cancer, mental disease, heart disease and even the common cold.
There is another matter that I should like to bring before the committee, namely the question of old people. It is true that we have lengthened the span of life. New discoveries, new methods of treatment have gone a long way toward lengthening the span of life, but there will come a time when something happens, and it seems to be cardiovascular disease or cancer, that will ultimately carry them off. If we can make life better for these people of advanced age by new methods of treatment we should do everything possible to devise those methods.
I am concerned about the care of those elderly people. It is difficult to find some place where they can go when they become ill, when they become chronic invalids. We talked the other night on a bill about nursing homes. It is true that nursing homes are helping in a great way to take care of many of those people, but on the other hand you will find them in the hospitals possibly suffering from some chronic disease without

hope of recovery. There is no place else to put them, and they are occupying beds which possibly could be put to use for acute cases, if there were some places in which those chronic cases could be properly attended. Hospitals seem to lack care for those suffering from chronic diseases, and especially those in the older groups.
There is another matter at which we should take a second look, and that is the legislation concerning old age pensions. Under present conditions I find people writing to me very often stating that they find it very difficult to get along on $40 a month. Sometimes I feel that some of those who are trying to get along on $40 a month are suffering from malnutrition.
So far as hospitals are concerned, there still remains a demand for beds. It is expensive to build hospitals even with the grants given by the federal and provincial governments. The question of the cost of hospital care still remains before us. To the individual who seeks a private room, a semi-private room or even ward care, hospitalization is a very expensive procedure; and not only that, but hospital boards throughout the country are continually trying to balance their ledgers and they find it extremely difficult to finance their institutions.
One other matter I will discuss at brief length is the question of the shortage of nurses. I do not believe the shortage is as extreme as it has been at previous times. The minister has always told us this is a provincial matter. It is perfectly true that the training of nurses comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but I think something further could be done by the federal government in view of the large number of nurses employed by that government. The federal government requires nurses for its veterans hospitals and for the institutions which come under the care of the minister. T.C.A. also require a large number of them. Because the federal government requires so many nurses for its various branches I feel that something could be done by this government by way of grants to assist some of the institutions which find it difficult to train nurses.
I have one other matter for the attention of the Minister of Finance. From time to time we have an application from someone who is importing some of the new drugs from the United States. There have been concessions made, and I was very glad when the matter of oxygen received consideration by the department. There are still drugs, however, which are available in the United States at a much lower price than that for which we can obtain them here in Canada. These drugs are continually used by physicians. If they
Supply-Health and Welfare accomplish something in the way of relief or cure I think we could very well do something to reduce the price of those drugs by bringing them into the country free of any duty or anything else which contributes toward making them more expensive for the patients who require them.
I have one other matter to discuss, and I realize it is not the concern of this committee in so far as legislation is concerned; that is the question of accident prevention. This matter has been before the house before. Last winter we were all alarmed at the tremendous number of children who were burned in fires throughout the whole of Canada and particularly in and near the city of Ottawa, where the matter was constantly brought to our attention. I do not know if there is any legislation regarding the electrical wiring of houses or fire prevention that would do something to cut down this high rate of mortality from burning, but if there is something that can be done we should do it. If nothing can be done in the way of legislation, would the minister put out pamphlets and advertisements and carry on a definite campaign concerning this matter?
Another aspect of the same subject is the question of highway accidents. I realize that to some extent this matter comes under the Criminal Code, but our rate of accidents in Canada is becoming simply ghastly, and in some way all governments must work together to stop this tremendous mortality rate on the highways of our country. I remember producing statistics in this house two years ago, I think, that revealed our bad record in this country compared with other countries in the world in the matter of highway fatalities. If anything can be done by consultation among the provincial governments or through legislation originating in this parliament, I suggest we should co-bperate with the other legislative bodies in doing everything we can to decrease the rate of mortality among children and adults who are burned in fires and the number of people killed as a result of highway accidents.
I may have other statements to make on particular items, and I shall defer any criticism or contributions I wish to make until that time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are now dealing with the estimates of one of the oldest departments of government in this country, and I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say we are dealing with the estimates of one of the most important departments of government. Indeed, he is favoured in having the responsibility of presiding over the affairs of the Department of National Health and Welfare.

Supply-Health and Welfare
As one who is sometimes known as a severe critic of the minister and the government for the snail's pace with which it deals with matters that come under the general heading of health and welfare, I want to say that we in this group are proud of the extent to which we have made some progress in this field in Canada.
It is now recognized-and this is a departure from the days when the British North America Act was framed and the word "health" was not even mentioned in it-that the health of the Canadian people is a social responsibility and therefore a responsibility of government. It has also been recognized by this parliament that economic security, particularly with respect to contingencies over which people have no control, such as old age, is also a responsibility of the legislative bodies of Canada. We have recognized that responsibility in a way of which we in this group are particularly proud; namely that we have established in Canada the principle of universality with respect to old age pensions, at least for those 70 years of age and over, and with respect to family allowances.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, although we welcome the progress that has been made in Canada, we are extremely critical of the government and of the minister who presides over this department for what we feel to be an attitude that the job is done. It seems to me that what the minister and this government need to learn is a very simple truth that was brought home to Alice in Wonderland; namely, that there are times when you have to run as fast as you can just to keep up with where you are.
The minister and the government, particularly since old age pensions were put on the new basis represented in the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act, seem to feel that all of us on this side of the house and all the people in the country should from this point on just praise the government for what has been done. The government seems unable to realize that time is moving on and problems such as those facing our senior citizens, and problems in the field of health such as those which have been outlined so capably by my friend the hon. member for Lanark, require serious attention and action at a much faster pace than they are getting from this government.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, I want to suggest to the government in the words of a pamphlet which I have on my desk and to which I made reference in the committee on estimates, that the time has come for a new look in welfare. That phrase, "the new look in welfare", was the title of an address given


recently in Toronto by Professor John Morgan of the school of social work at the University of Toronto.
I indicated in the committee on estimates when we were dealing with these matters that Professor Morgan's thesis, if I do him justice by trying to boil down a lecture into two or three sentences, is that the time has come to realize that welfare is not just a matter of rescuing the underprivileged but rather it should be seen as a case of the mutual dependency of all individuals in our highly organized society. At one point in his lecture Professor Morgan referred to a phrase which is quite common, namely the welfare state, and suggested that it might be an improvement on that phraseology to speak of the "socially responsible state". I think hon. members will recognize what Professor Morgan has in mind in suggesting that change.
There is perhaps a tendency, at any rate on the part of some of those who talk of the welfare state, to think of programs of public welfare as programs for rescuing the underprivileged. Let it be said categorically that so' long as there is one underprivileged person in the country it is the job of society to try to rescue that person. But Professor Morgan makes the point that in our highly organized society there should be a recognition that there is a mutuality of responsibility and a situation of interdependence which can be more accurately apprehended under the title of a "socially responsible state".
It is that new look which I should like to urge upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare, upon the government, upon this parliament, and indeed upon the people of Canada who are interested in these problems. As I have already suggested, let us never fail in our responsibility toward the underprivileged, toward those in need, but at the same time let us recognize that we have a tremendous opportunity with the tremendous wealth that we are capable of producing in this modern age to organize our society on the basis of mutual interdependence in such a way that all members of the community, all members of society, may enjoy health and economic security.
Some of those who attack expenditures on health and social security seem still to have the notion that programs under these headings are simply programs to give something to certain individuals. We suggest that the proper approach to health and welfare programs in this day and age is to see in them a general or co-operative sharing of the wealth we are able to produce in such a way that all our people will have decent mini-mums of health care, decent minimums of

social security and be able to enjoy life to the full as we believe it is possible in this modern age.
Toward that end I urge upon the government, using again the words "new look", that it reconsider the whole question of our old age security. As I say, the Minister of National Health and Welfare seems to feel that because we are paying at the federal level pensions of $40 per month to all Canadians 70 years of age and over, that because we are paying at the federal level half the cost of pensions on a means test basis to those between the ages of 65 and 69 years, that is enough for the time being. I suggest that anyone who takes that approach is looking at welfare on the old basis, as a case of handing out money solely on the basis that there are underprivileged who are in need.
We contend that it should be the aim of our old age security program to share with the senior citizens in any generation the wealth which is being created at that time, the volume of which is due in part to what the senior citizens did in their working days to build up the country. You do not recognize that principle by the payment of only $40 per month at 70 years of age and only $40 a month between the ages of 65 and 69 years on a means test basis.
I shall perhaps have more to say on this when we reach the particular item in the estimates, but I want to lay it before the minister and before the government at this point, as one of the most important items to which attention should be given, that the time has come for a substantial increase in the amount of the old age pension and for the removal of the means test at age 65.
As everyone knows, we have witnessed in recent years a tremendous increase in our gross national product. It was something of the order of $16-4 billion in 1949, and I take that year because that is the year in which $40 was first set as the amount of the federal old age pension. The predictions are that this year it will be of the order of $28 billion. That is an increase of more than 70 per cent. Although from 1949 until the present we have witnessed an increase to the extent of 70 per cent in the gross national product of this country, we are still paying to our senior citizens the same amount of pension we paid in 1949. It is true that certain changes have been made in the meantime, in that the pension has been put on a universal basis and the age of eligibility has been changed, albeit with the means test; nevertheless the amount our older people get out of the federal treasury or as a result of federal legislation 67509-412
Supply-Health and Welfare is still the same as when our gross national product was considerably less than it is at the present time.
That is not in keeping with what I have referred to as the new look in welfare. That is not in keeping with Professor Morgan's phrase, "a socially responsible state". The greater wealth we are producing today is due in part to those who are working today, but it is due also in part to what our older people did in the decades gone by in helping to build up this country. It is our contention that these older people who have helped to make possible what we are enjoying today should be given, not just enough to maintain a bare existence but a proper share in that greater wealth.
Toward that end we suggest that the increase in the amount of the old age pension should bear some relation to the increase in our gross national product. Since the amount of the old age pension was set at $40 there has been a 70 per cent increase on the one hand and we suggest that that should be matched by an increase of similar proportions on the other hand. If you take that figure the pension should be increased to $68 per month. We suggest that certainly it should not be less today than $60 or $65 a month, and we urge that on the government as strongly as we can.
Some of us were disappointed a week or so ago when we seemed to have difficulty getting out of the government a clear-cut statement as to what was going on in the government's mind regarding an increase in the old age pension. When the question was asked as to whether the government was planning to increase the old age pension at this or the next session the answer was, "No." When the question was asked whether the government was considering the plight and needs of our senior citizens, the answer was, "Yes." So the newspapers are confused; so the people of Canada are confused.
The difference between consideration and planning may be a case of splitting hairs which makes it possible for the government to give one answer to one question and another answer to the other, but we suggest that no society, no economy, is capable of making any boast unless it provides a decent medium of security for its older citizens. We say to those on the treasury benches that if they think they have any right to claim another vote of confidence from the people of this country, before they go to the people they must present to them a decent, adequate increase in the old age pension. We say it should be raised without delay to not less than $60 or $65 a month.
I share with the hon. member for Lanark the satisfaction that the estimates of this

Supply-Health and Welfare department were referred to the committee on estimates where we did have a very good discussion. Nevertheless when we discussed this matter in the committee the minister suggested that the provinces had some responsibility in this field as well as whatever responsibility the federal government might take. It is our contention that if you try to pass to the provinces responsibility for anything beyond $40 a month to our old age pensioners you are getting away from the principle of universality which the Minister of National Health and Welfare is so pleased about so far as old age pensions are concerned.
The provinces simply do not have the resources to pay pensions to everyone without a means test. If you pass the buck to the provinces so far as any increase in the pension is concerned you are asking for a reinstatement of the means test, at least with respect to that part of the pension, and I am sure the minister agrees with me that after the long struggle it took to get rid of the means test we do not want to go back to it. Yet to suggest that any additional amount of pension should be paid by the provinces is to ask for a reinstatement of the means test. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, that is one of the reasons I sought to speak about this the other day in the context of another matter. However, that debate is over.
But I say to the minister that he is not measuring up to his own responsibility in this field. He is not being consistent with his pleasure that the federal government has accepted the principle of universality. When that principle is endorsed in other countries the minister is always glad to note it. He is always pleased when in the United States or in some European countries bouquets are given to Canada for the fact that we pay a pension without a means test, but I say the minister is not being consistent with his satisfaction over that fact when he replies to us that the provinces should take over from the $40 figure in so far as any additional amount is concerned.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I lay that before the government on behalf of this group just as strongly as I can. I am conscious of the fact that I am laying this before the government not many months in advance of an occasion when the government will probably go to the people of the country. I say that if they are going to the people of Canada, to whom they owe their responsibility, before they do so they should indicate clearly what they are going to do in the important field of old age pensions.
As I indicated earlier in borrowing a few thoughts from Professor John Morgan, I feel that the idea of a new look in welfare also

calls for a new approach to the whole question of health care. We all listened with interest to the speech made a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Lanark, and I am sure he too would agree with this quotation, which is in line with some of the things he said. I quote from Professor Morgan:
It seems clear to me that the socially responsible state must necessarily recognize an overriding responsibility for insuring that as many people in the community get as much health care-notice I say health care and not disease cure-as can effectively be arranged.
If we are going to take a new look at the health of the nation, if we are going to recognize that this is a responsibility just as great as if not greater than some of the things we do under the heading of defence production, which we were talking about earlier, or under the heading of trade and commerce or under the heading of finance-and I suggest, and I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare will agree with me, that when we are talking about the health of the people of the country we are talking about something that is far more important than these other matters-we have to strike out much more boldly than the government has done up to the present time.
I am aware of the proposals made to the provinces by the federal government as a result of the meetings held in Ottawa in January of this year. As I said in the committee on estimates, we of this group welcome those proposals as a step in the right direction. To have them put into effect would certainly bring about a better situation than that existing at the present time. There are certain things that are good about those proposals. In any province in which they would come into effect the principle of universality of such hospital care as is provided would be established. A portion, though in our view not a sufficiently large portion, of the cost of hospital care is to be paid for, according to the proposals, out of the federal treasury, and to the extent that that amount is paid out of the federal treasury there is some recognition of the principle of paying according to ability to pay.
But, Mr. Chairman, in our view the proposals do not go far enough. In the first place they cover only hospital care and one or two other matters. They do not cover some of the major items of health care. The government's proposals are not set up on a basis that gives us the hope that within a reasonable time they will be extended to all the people of Canada from coast to coast, in whatever province they live. The sharing of the cost is not on a basis that puts enough of the cost on the federal treasury where costs are met according to ability to pay,

rather than according to the illness that people happen to suffer. There are also other shortcomings, such as the failure to provide coverage for people in mental institutions and others in similar categories.
Nevertheless we would like to see a start made. We regret that so far only three provinces have agreed to the plan whereas the government requires six representing a sufficient number of people to constitute a majority of the population of Canada. But we suggest that one of the reasons for the slowness on the part of the provinces is that the federal government has not measured up to its own responsibilities in this field, has not played a role consistent with the talking it has been doing in the field of health insurance for many years.
I am not going to go back again to that ancient year when the Liberal party first started talking about health insurance. Everyone knows what year it was. There are a number of members in the house now who were not even born when the Liberal party first advocated health insurance. But I would remind the minister, who is proud of the proposals that he has been in a position to make to the provinces this year, that some pretty striking publicity was given to moves made by this government some time ago. I hold in my hand a copy of the Ottawa Journal which is getting a bit yellow. The date is Tuesday, March 16, 1943; in other words it is over 13 years old. The main heading reads, "Billion Dollar Yearly Outlay Required for Post-War Social Security Plans". Look at the next heading: "Health Insurance Bills Provide Medical and Dental Care." Over in the right-hand column in the main story I find that it says:
A gigantic pooling of Canada's doctors' bills was proposed today by pensions minister Mackenzie in draft health insurance bills submitted at the first meeting of the special House of Commons committee on social security. Health insurance was presented as a concrete measure for study by the committee but the minister also submitted a report on a general plan for social security which would involve retirement pensions, revisions of the present old age pensions and unemployment insurance systems, children's allowances and funeral allowances, as well as health insurance.
Then spelling out what had been laid before parliament, here is another article on the front page under the heading "Still Have Choice of Doctor Under Health Insurance Plan". Then over here in another column I find the highlights of the proposals of that day, and this is a reference to the Marsh report which was laid before parliament at that time. There are eight or ten proposals set out and one of them is this:
Institute free medical care for all citizens.
67509-412J
Supply-Health and Welfare
I well remember when this paper came out. In fact I was so greatly interested in it that obviously I saved it so I would have it in future years to look back and remember that on that day the Ottawa Journal came out and told us the news, that health insurance was before us as a concrete measure just around the corner.
Mr. Chairman, the Ottawa Journal was not off the beam in what its columns said about draft bills, because at least one draft bill was prepared. I have a copy of it in my hand. The date at the top is April 26, 1944. It is marked "Draft Bill". It was actually tabled in the House of Commons in August of that year, but that is as far as the government went with it. The long title of the bill is as follows:
An act respecting health insurance, public health, the conservation of health and the prevention of disease.
Clause 1 reads as follows:
This act may be cited as the national health act.
It is a bill of some 43 pages, spelling out in detail the mechanics for setting up national health insurance. That was back in 1944. Incidentally, this particular bill was available to certain candidates in the 1945 election, as indeed there have been other items and documents through the years to show that the Liberals stand for health insurance. There is no doubt about that. The Liberals stand for health insurance and they have been standing for it for a long time. But they seem to have the opinion that by assuring the people that they stand for it, by promising them that something is going to be done, by making proposals to the provinces, the people will keep on putting them back here, counting on the government doing something about it.
We welcome the proposals the minister made to the provinces this year, despite their shortcomings about which I shall have something to say later. But my fear is this, and it is a fear that has been developing in the last two or three months as time has gone by with no more than three provinces agreeing. My fear is that the government has made these proposals requiring the concurrence of at least six provinces, including either Ontario or Quebec, hoping that the making of these proposals will do as a health insurance plank for another federal election.
I submit, Mr. Chairman-and I think the minister knows it-that he cannot face the people of Canada in another election unless something is done. I am sure the minister knows that in order to convince the people of Canada that something is going to be done, these proposals must be revised and improved to the point where they will be

Supply

Health and Welfare more acceptable to the provinces, so that the required six or more will come into the arrangement.
I plead with the minister and the government, as I did with respect to old age pensions, to face up to the seriousness of this problem. I care not whether our gross national product is $28 billion, $48 billion or $108 billion; I care not about the buildings, the highways or the other things that we may produce as marks of our great civilization. If we are not able to take care of the health of our people, on both a curative and preventive basis; if we are not able to make sure that our people get health care because they need it, whether or not they have the money with which to pay for it, just as we insist that every child gets an education regardless of the income of his parents, I say that our economy has nothing to boast about.
I urge that the minister and the government take a new look at these proposals, at this health insurance scheme which seems to have bogged down. I urge that following that new look some modifications and improvements be made so we might very soon have the enactment of this health insurance plank that has been promised across the years. I am indebted to Professor Morgan, as I have already said, for the phrase that I have used more or less as the theme of my remarks today, namely the need for a new look in welfare.
I call upon the government to take a new look at these two important problems of old age security and the health of our people, and to put into the solution of these problems enough will and determination and enough money to see to it that our people have decent security in their older years, and that all the people in this country have the health care they deserve.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to follow the two previous speakers in the request for greater and improved health services. I believe everyone in this house is quite sincere in asking that that situation be brought about. However, in so far as the last speaker is concerned, that is just about as far as he and I are in agreement. I certainly cannot agree with the method by which he wants that situation brought into effect.
I listened with a good deal of interest to the hon. member for Lanark, as I always do when he speaks on health matters. He speaks with sincerity, and of course he also speaks from professional knowledge that we as laymen do not possess. But in looking at this department we must realize that an extremely large amount of money is involved, namely over $70 million. Yet it is

not a matter of dollars and cents alone. In the committee on estimates this department received careful consideration, and I believe we worked co-operatively. I know the minister and the officials of his department co-operated to the fullest degree with us. Some 370 printed pages were devoted to the proceedings of this committee, and many of the matters were discussed at length. I therefore feel that it is unnecessary to go into them in any great detail today.
Health is a national problem, Mr. Chairman. I do not think anyone disputes that statement. So long as federal taxes constitute the lion's share of taxation in this country-
I believe about 72 per cent-a large measure of responsibility must rest on the shoulders of the national government. In saying that I am not saying I am in agreement with the method of taxation and with the need of having that procedure of health and welfare care followed. We must realize that it is policies such as that under which we are working, and we must govern ourselves accordingly. But as I say, national assistance is becoming more and more necessary. At the same time, however, we must have co-operation between the central or national government and the provinces.
I am glad to note that throughout the entire proceedings of our committee the minister of this department and every one of his officials expressed a keen desire to work with the provinces in a wide-open spirit of co-operation. So long as that spirit prevails there is not too much fear from central domination or central control.
I should like to refer in a general way to the national hospital assistance plan. However, I do not think I need to say any more than the few words which I said in committee. I realize that this, speaking of the national hospital plan, is an interim step and I do not believe we should look for perfection at this time. We are bound to find that there are some difficulties and we shall meet some problems that will have to be ironed out.
Now, there are possibly some problems within the framework of this proposed scheme, but I am confident that with the spirit of co-operation which the minister evidenced in his appearances before the committee there should not be too much difficulty along those lines. Some of us were disappointed that assistance was not provided for the care of mental cases. Of course I think that resulted more from the fact that we were not correctly informed. I understand that mental cases being cared for in hospitals will be treated as ordinary hospital patients, and a share of the cost

of looking after those patients will be provided. Of course those in institutions will not be a responsibility of the federal department.
Then we must realize, as was so well pointed out by the hon. member for Lanark, that the thinking of the medical profession today is directed more toward preventive medicine than to the cure or treatment of disease. Of course we cannot neglect treatment; we cannot let these people die without attention. But I believe that over a long period of years we will derive more benefit from every dollar that we can possibly channel into research work and into every known means of preventing disease. I was glad to see that there is a lot of money-I am not going to say it is enough- being contributed by this government along those lines. For instance, commencing in 1948-49 there have been grants from the national treasury for the care of crippled children totalling $129,676. There has been $2,208,016 given toward mental health.
The hon. member for Lanark mentioned the system of control and checking in connection with tuberculosis. We have practically eliminated that disease. There has been a contribution of $611,573 toward that. Then there is the very important field of public health research. " It is something that I should like to see expanded very widely. There has been a contribution of $2,415,016 toward that. Then for general public health the contribution amounted to $1,566,944. Child and maternal health is another very important field that has been given a lot of consideration. We have prenatal care and infant care today such as was not dreamed of, and I think the smaller death loss in infancy can be attributed in no small measure to advances in these two fields. So we have a total of $6,999,364, and that does not include a grant of $682,966 to the cancer control institute.
We are asking for larger grants, and of course that is human nature. We are never satisfied with what we are getting. However, there is no point in making grants, Mr. Chairman, unless the facilities are available to make use of these grants. We find in another table that of the total that has been allocated, $6,999,364, the total expenditure during that period was $5,775,271. I feel that every person in this house will agree that if the various departments of health in the provinces and the various research centres throughout Canada had the facilities to use the total amount of money which was allocated, they would certainly have used it and been crying for more. Here we see that there is over $1 million, almost a million and a quarter, of the amount that was
Supply-Health and Welfare made available which these various institutions were not able to use. Therefore I would certainly recommend that every effort be made to enlarge the facilities in this important field of research and preventive medicine. Then when we have got to the stage where we are able to use all the money which is made available, it is time for us to start hollering for more money.
Of course we realize that there are some steps being taken to increase the number of pupils who are taking advantage of professional training. The hon. member for Lanark mentioned mental illness, and perhaps the greatest shortage of trained technical and professional men and women is in that field. However, I am glad to see that steps are being taken to provide scholarships and financial assistance, as well as training centres, where these people can get the necessary instruction if they so desire.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a few words about welfare. We have had quite a demand for the new look in welfare. I do not think any of us feel that our senior citizens and our disabled, no matter for what reason, are being properly cared for. Again I am going to put on the record a few words which I said in committee in dealing with this subject. "I know we will all agree it is a disgrace, in a country with the gross national product and the gross national income which we have, to expect people to live on $480 a year. It is just proof of the fact that the time has come when we have to take a new look at it and give further consideration to those who are dependent entirely on it."
I think those last words, Mr. Chairman will give you an idea of our thinking along those lines. We do not like the sound of that word "universality", and we do not like this system of transfer payments to everyone when they reach a certain age. On the other hand, we are firmly convinced that those who are unable to earn their own living whether it be through age, sickness or disability, must be provided for by society. And, of course, the only way in which that is done, or can be done, is through some sort of national scheme in co-operation-and again I stress the word "co-operation"-with the provinces.
Since I come from the province of British Columbia I am proud to say that our people in the categories I have just mentioned are cared for a little better than the national average, but we realize that even that is not good enough. I would make a special plea to the minister that the pensions across Canada for those unable to earn their own living, regardless of the cause, should be brought up to a standard which would allow

Supply-Health and Welfare them something that is in keeping with the productive capacity of this great country of Canada.
I would like to make a special plea for the blind in a word or two, in closing. This class of afflicted persons has special problems. Seeing-eye services are required. There are personal appliances that are available for them; there are appliances for use in their homes that are available to blind persons and I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that some provision should be made under which those blind people would be given a fund to purchase the many things which would make their way of life much easier and much brighter.

Mr. Chairman, one thing I think we will all agree has become very clear during the last few years is that the $40 old age pension is inadequate to provide a livelihood for our older citizens. I think every hon. member is familiar with cases of older people who are experiencing real hardship today, and the increasing cost of living is making the situation grow worse as time goes on.
Since the pension was first introduced in 1950, its value in terms of the things it will buy has been steadily decreasing, with the result that today you must spend $45.70 to buy the same amount of food, clothing, heat, rent and the other necessities of life that you could buy for $40 when the pension was first introduced. That means, Mr. Chairman, that in terms of things it would buy in 1950 a $40 pension today is worth only $34.30. In another 10 years, at the present rate of inflation, the value of the pension will have been reduced still further until it is worth only $25.
In addition to the inadequacy of the pension as a means of support for people over 70 years of age, another very serious problem is that faced by workers who reach the age of 65 and are retired, and for whom no pension plan has been available to which they could contribute during their working years, and by which they could support themselves and their families when they are retired.
Some firms have pension plans but unfortunately the great majority do not, and when most workers are retired at 65, they have only the savings which they have been able to lay aside during their working years, after meeting the many obligations which families encounter from time to time. Often a lingering illness or serious accident has reduced those savings to a point where there is little left to live on after the breadwinner of the family has retired. I think we all agree it is obvious that some better method must be found for bridging the gap between 65 and 70 years of age, and for bringing our old age pension more into line with the needs of the great majority of the people who receive it.
The question is, of course, how can this desirable end best be accomplished? I believe, sir, that the social security system in operation in the United States offers a practical means of providing such a plan, and supplementing our basic $40 old age pension so that our people may look forward to their later years without fear of hunger, cold, or lack of the primary necessities of life.
Supply-Health and Welfare
For the past 20 years the United States has had in operation a contributory social security program which is paid for by contributions from employers, employees, and the self-employed. The way this plan operates has been very well outlined in an excellent pamphlet entitled "20 years of social security" issued by the United States department of health, education and welfare, social security administration, under code No. OASI-26-C, August, 1955.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that the United States is giving consideration to adopting our old age security plan?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, after reading this pamphlet, I would be very surprised if they are. They might be using some features of our social security plan, but it seems to me the social security program outlined in this pamphlet is a very excellent one, and bears consideration. I know from talking to quite a number of workers in the United States that the plan is very popular with the people in that country.
Under this program, when a worker's earnings cease due to retirement at 65 years of age or later, monthly cash benefits are paid to the worker. If he dies, monthly cash benefits are paid to his survivors. Today nine out of ten people living in the United States who work for a living can look forward to receiving retirement benefits from the federal social security program, and nine out of ten mothers and children are assured of receiving monthly cash benefits upon the death of the breadwinner of the family.
When this program started 20 years ago, only those employed in commerce and industry were eligible to participate in it. However, in 1950 and 1954, amendments were passed by the United States congress which extended the coverage of this program to most self-employed people in business, on farms, and in certain professions, and also to hired farm workers and domestic workers as well.
By the end of 1954, the monthly average payment to a retired worker with no dependents was $56.50. To a retired aged couple it was $98.50. To aged widows it was $46; and to widowed mothers with two children it was $126. These figures are averages for all beneficiaries. Payments are higher for those who have more recently come on the rolls, and whose benefits are based on earnings from 1950 on. Among these, the average monthly benefit paid to a retired worker with no dependents is $76; an aged couple, $128; an aged widow, $65; and a young widow with two minor children, $180. There is also a lump sum paid to a worker's survivors, varying from $90 to $225, and obviously designed

Supply-Health and Welfare to pay funeral and other expenses that occur at the time a person dies.
I	think it is interesting to note that the year 1950, the time from which one can qualify for this latest series of payments I have mentioned, was the same year when our present old age pension plan came into operation, which pays $40 at 70 years of age, and provides no survivors' benefits.
Under the provisions of the 1954 amendment, a United States worker who meets certain work requirements may preserve his benefit rights during a prolonged period of total disability, by having his earning record frozen. When that record is frozen, the period during which he is disabled and receiving little or no earnings does not count in determining the amount of work required for payments, or in figuring the average monthly earnings from which the amount of the benefit is figured.
Money to pay for old age and survivors' insurance comes from social security contributions, paid by employees, employers, and the self-employed. These contributions are paid into a special trust fund which can only pay out benefits and the cost of administering the program. These contributions amount to
2	per cent for employers and employees, and
3	per cent for the self-employed, on earnings up to $4,200 a year. The cost of administering the program amounts to 2 per cent of total contributions.
I believe these figures give us an idea of the social security coverage which a United States workman receives in return for the payment of 2 per cent of his wages.
Let us now see what his Canadian counterpart pays and receives. First of all, the Canadian workman pays 2 per cent additional income tax, and an extra 2 per cent sales tax on practically everything he buys. In return he receives a pension limited to $40, for which he has to wait five years longer than his United States counterpart. If he should die, there are no survivor benefits whatsoever.
Thus we can see that the Canadian workman pays considerably more than his United States counterpart, and receives considerably less social security coverage in return. For these reasons, I submit that the United States social security program should be given very serious study by this government as a means of making available to Canadians, first of all, a contributory retirement pension at 65 years of age; second, survivors' benefits for dependents; and, third, adding sufficient to our old age pension so that our people can look forward to their later years with confidence and peace of mind.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Everybody in this house knows what it costs for food and for the necessities of life. This is particularly true in the case of old people who refuse to enter religious institutions, preferring to live on their own income, in spite of the sacrifices they have to make.
Many old couples, after living long years together, cannot bring themselves to part, even if they realize that they are reaching the end of their days.
As to those who have already lost a life-mate, or who have never married and thus have nobody to offer them a home, they have to face reality and enter an institution or home for the aged where they spend the remainder of their lives.
While in the various religious institutions like those I have in my county, and the others that are found in my province, they receive what I would call a mother's care and attention from the devoted nuns who are responsible for them, the amount those old people receive is far from adequate.

I wish to take this opportunity to pay a heartfelt and deserved tribute to all those dedicated souls, particularly in my county, who spend their lives trying to bring more happiness and serenity to those old men and women whose pilgrimage is about to end. I want to take a tew minutes of the time of the committee to discuss what I feel is a very important expansion or proposed expansion of the functions of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I refer, of course, to the proposed national hospital insurance scheme.
I think I should take the opportunity to make it clear, at least to those in my constituency for whom I am concerned, that a rather difficult constitutional problem exists with regard to the implementation of a national hospital insurance scheme. I do not know whether the public generally realize that we have no constitutional authority to enter into the field, and that this is a matter that requires the co-operation, as has been said previously by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and by the Prime Minister, of at least a majority of the provinces.
I am particularly concerned here because I feel that the scheme can never be instituted unless my own province, Ontario, decides to take part in it. I think that proposition is generally accepted. We are a populous province. We are quite a rich province. In order to make a practical job of instituting such a scheme; in order to ensure that there will be sufficient participation in the scheme; and in order to make it at all financially practical to institute such a scheme I feel, and I think most hon. members will agree, it is necessary to have Ontario participate.
A procedure was adopted at the series of federal-provincial conferences in April of 1955 and October of 1955 whereby representations were made to the federal government by the provinces, and in turn discussions were carried on by the federal government with regard to several matters, among which was included this national health insurance program. I for one was rather optimistic after the conferences as to the future of our activities in this field. As I recall the conferences, particularly the October conference, the representatives of Ontario, led by the premier of that province, came forward with what I felt was a comprehensive suggestion for a national hospital scheme.
For the benefit of hon. members I should like to recall just a short excerpt from the representations he made to the conference.
I am quoting from page 24 of the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference, 1955, of October 3 last. The premier of Ontario made the following remarks:
It is beyond question that a comprehensive plan requires both federal and provincial participation. 67509-413J
Supply-Health and Welfare In its proposals of 1945, the federal government set its participation at 60 per cent.
