We know the wealth of the country is created day by day by the labours of the men and women of this country applied to our natural resources. It can increase, and it is increasing. The fact that our gross national product has increased so tremendously in the past 10 years is a matter which should give most Canadians some pride; but the majority of people who have passed their three score years and ten are denied the right to share in that increased production.

I have a copy of "Age and Opportunity", an excellent study prepared by the welfare council of greater Winnipeg. They propose a monthly budget which I think most people will probably consider not too extravagant for a city like Winnipeg. They consider that a couple should have not $80 a month, but they should have each month $40 for rent; $60 for food; $20 for clothing; $4 for church; $6 for medical, insurance or care. Then they should have $10 for hobbies and membership-I suppose that would include newspapers-$9 for transportation; $10 for incidentals; $4 for laundry. This totals $167.
I feel that no member in this chamber can view with satisfaction the fact that such a large number of our fellow citizens are paid $80 when some of the ablest authorities in Winnipeg think they should have $167. They come up with a budget for the individual that is just half, $83.50 per month. They point out that two-thirds of the aged in greater Winnipeg are living on incomes that are marginal or less. No one can put any responsibility on the C.C.F. for the fact that two-thirds of the aged in greater Winnipeg are living on something that is marginal or less.
The pamphlet, "Fourteen days as an old age pensioner", describes life in Toronto the good. I suggest that the minister, who has been a friend of mine for many years since we were both private members and were not able to afford to stay in the Chateau, but shared quarters in a home in Ottawa which was not as expensive as the Chateau, should come along with me-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are getting very old.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-and I would be glad to go along with the minister for two weeks so he could check on me and I could check on him, and we would try doing what this young reporter for the Toronto Star, William MacEachern, did. He describes in this way:
My existence for the next two weeks will depend on a one-burner hotplate, a frying pan, a teapot, $20 and my own resourcefulness.
Monday morning I move into an unheated stark, 2x4 cubicle on the edge of Toronto's slum empire, and for the next 14 days I will try to lead the life of an old-age pensioner. In my pocket will be $20-
May I invite the hon. member for York-Scarborough who is younger than we are to join us.
-the amount most pensioners receive over a two-week period; with this I will have to pay for my room, eat and entertain myself.
My room will cost me $5 a week, which means that I will have $10 to keep body and soul together for these two weeks.
Small and bare as my room is, it is by far the cheapest and by far the most acceptable of 39 places I visited in the city's so-called cheaper
Supply-Health and Welfare rooming house section. I also received 68 answers to an ad in the Star last weekend. In the ad I said I was a pensioner and wanted a light housekeeping room.
Only one-the one I eventually accepted-was under $6. Seventy-five per cent were over $10 and the rest were around $8.
At first I didn't give the callers any explanation but listened patiently while they extolled the virtues of their accommodations: ''Nice, clean room, fully furnished, quiet, in a nice section of town," and so on.
It's all over.
This morning at 10 o'clock-14 days, $19.98 and Ilf pounds after I began my ordeal as an old age pensioner-I walked out of my mothball mansion, out of the hotplate jungle, back into a world of satisfying meals, regular pay cheques and happy, fast-fleeting hours.
Behind me are two of the most memorable weeks of my life, two weeks spent slavishly worrying over little, petty, insignificant things-at least they seem petty and insignificant now but at the time they were the most important things in my life-trying to squeeze the last iota of purchasing power out of my dollars, quibbling over dimes and nickels and even pennies and scrounging and scrimping here, there and everywhere.	~
Gone are the niggardly, skinflint, pinchpenny days when a nickel for a newspaper was wanton extravagance, a dime for street car fare was out of the question, and a walk around town was an evening's entertainment.
Well, that is enough, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would be willing to try.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member who has interrupted would be willing to try for two weeks, as this young reporter did.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would be willing to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the hon. member, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the hon. member for York-Scarborough would be willing to try it, I am sure the four of us would come back here with a very different attitude from what we have now toward the people of Canada who are forced to live day after day, week after week, year after year on $40 a month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How many million people are living under worse conditions?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am aware of that; I am aware that in India, in China, in Burma and in a great many other countries people are having even worse times than our old age pensioners, but our old age pensioners are squeezed down to a niggardly $40 a month at a time when our corporation profits are higher than they have ever been in Canadian history.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think that those who are squeezing them down are-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member can make his speech on old age pensions after I am through. My time is limited. I did not hear the question, Mr. Chairman. My time is limited and I want to-

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Come back.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, I shall be glad to come back when we reach the item, but I want to discuss the question of health as it affects the people of Canada. I was not surprised at the remarks made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, but no one in this day and age can establish the fact that good health is not a matter of national concern; the quality of the health services must not be measured by one's bank account.
Let me remind the committee that when war broke out we passed legislation that compelled the young people of this country to place their services at the disposal of Canada, and in due course we drafted mobilization regulations. I hold in my hand Hansard for November 11, 1941. At page 4427 the then minister of national war services, now Judge Thorson, placed before us a table showing the percentage of young Canadians of military age in the different categories in the different districts in Canada. Most people nowadays cannot quite realize, following those 10 years of depression, that 44-1 per cent of the young lads in the prime of life failed to get into category A. They were in other categories, B-l, B-2, C-l and C-2 and all down the line. Out of 209,298 called up there were 92,498 young Canadians rejected for military service in 1941 because they could not measure up to the standards that were thought desirable for military service at that time.
I realize that the regulations were changed later, and I also realize that there are many men who have disabilities which prevent them getting into A category who can do many other useful things. While I cannot prove it, I am sure that a great many of those 92,498 were rejected because they had been forced to live on relief budgets. In my area $5 a month, plus $1 per month per child, was the amount considered ample during those terrible 1930's. Therefore I submit, Mr. Chairman, that in wartime or in peacetime no nation can accept the situation that I have just described when such a large percentage are rejected for military service.
The hon. member across the way suggests that there are countries where conditions are worse than they are in Canada. That is quite right. I hold in my hand the book entitled, "The War On World Poverty" written by Harold Wilson. He gives some statistics for all the major countries of the world. These statistics are not right up to date; this book was written in 1953. Canadian figures are a little better at the moment. I think the figures for infant mortality can be accepted as a fair criteria of the general health of the people in the various countries. One

can see that Canada is in a much better position than Formosa, for example, which has an infant mortality rate of 125 for every 1,000 live births. Korea has 115; Burma, 203. Canada has a much better record, of course. Canada's rate at that time was 42-8; but let me tell the committee that the United States, New Zealand, Switzerland, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Australia and Norway had much better records than Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What are their rates?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give them. The rate for the United States is 31-1; New Zealand, 23-8; Switzerland, 34-3; Sweden, 23-2; the United Kingdom, 34-1; Denmark, 35-3; Australia, 23 [DOT] 3; and Norway, 29 [DOT] 6. There are a great many countries that have worse records than we have. I submit that our very rich country, with our broad spaces, with our trained personnel, cannot be proud of the fact that she is so far down the line in connection with such an important question as infant mortality.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre apparently are paving the way for some retreat in this important field of a national health insurance plan.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member with all the vigour at my command that the government is not in any way retreating, but is anxiously awaiting the replies of the provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that statement. I wish the minister had made the statement before the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre spoke.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend has referred several times to the fact that I have not spoken. I felt that we would make more progress if we waited until we reached the item. There is an item for health insurance, and I will be prepared-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Why did the minister not suggest that to the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have already suggested it to several other hon. members, and I would be prepared to expand on our proposal and deal with some of the points that have been raised. It seems to me, if I can make a suggestion, that we have had a good general discussion, and I did think that was the right place and that I should give some leadership myself in that connection. That is the only reason. I am very anxious to discuss this particular question of the federal proposal on the matter of hospital insurance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am sure we are all very glad to hear the

minister any time he rises, but I want to assure him he is not closing me off at this point. I have here an interesting table which the minister presented to our committee. I think the hon. member for York-Scarborough should consult the proceedings of this committee. The information which has been compiled regarding the estimated cost of the proposed national hospital scheme is quite extensive, and I think they make the proposal so attractive that no province in Canada would stay out of this scheme.
The minister gave us figures for the provinces. I have not checked all of these. He also gave an estimate of what the people in the various provinces pay through Blue Cross and other non-profit plans and through private insurance companies. There is also an estimate of what people pay for hospital care in some 510 out of 855 general hospitals in Canada. This last figure is not complete, and the conclusions I am drawing are certainly on the conservative side.
This table points out, for example, that the province of Nova Scotia is now spending over $5-4 million, the municipalities are spending $1-5 million and the people in Nova Scotia are paying $1,085,000 under Blue Cross, $500,000 to private insurance companies and $1,585,000 to hospitals. This suggests that the amount that would have to be raised in Nova Scotia is only $2,400,000. They are already paying $3,304,000 for services which would not be nearly as complete.
The province of Quebec is now paying over $13 million and the municipalities $4-8 million. It is estimated that Quebec would have to raise $27,400,000. But when you add the other figures I mentioned for Quebec, they are now spending $28,323,000; so the province would actually be saving money if one considers what is being paid to Blue Cross, to private insurance companies and the sum the citizens are now paying to their hospitals.
In Ontario the amount to be raised is $36,100,000. They are paying to Blue Cross $24,273,000, to private companies $11,835,000 and to hospitals $27,894,000. The amount that is needed in Ontario is $36,100,000 and they are now paying for other services $64 million, so I do not see how Ontario can possibly stay out of the scheme.
Concerning the province of Manitoba, I note that the people in that province are already paying $1,400,000 for hospital care. Municipalities are paying $2,200,000 and under Blue Cross over $3 million is being spent. Altogether they are paying $7,800,000 in Manitoba. All that would have to be raised in Manitoba would be $5,700,000. As you go across Canada province by province and
Supply-Health and Welfare take into account what is being paid to Blue Cross and insurance companies and to regular hospitals you find that the people in the provinces would be better off if their provinces reached an agreement with the federal government and the scheme was set up.
I want to say that while the proposal is a step in the right direction I feel this committee must not let the minister get away with his proposal to bar from the scheme over half the sick people in Canada, those who are suffering from tuberculosis and mental illnesses. I received an answer to a question on March 12 of this year. My question was as follows:
For the last year for which statistics are available of the number of patient days spent in Canadian hospitals, how many and what percentage were in the following: (a) mental hospitals; (b) psychiatric wards in hospitals; (c) T.B. hospitals; (d) public hospitals:	(e) federal hospitals; (f)
private hospitals?
The two groups the minister is barring in the mental and tuberculosis hospitals represent only 50 per cent of the sick population of this country who are ill every day of the year. They are to be barred from the benefits of this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that that is not a completely accurate statement?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Well, the minister can correct it. This was an answer that was brought down by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and these are the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics which were given to me. On the same day I had another question which read as follows:
For 1943 and 1953, what was the estimated cost per patient per day in the following hospitals: (a) mental; (b) T.B.; (c) public?
If you go back to 1943 you will find that we were spending in Canada 98 cents per person per day for the mentally ill. There has been an improvement, and we are now spending $2.70 per patient per day. Concerning people suffering from tuberculosis, in 1943 we were spending $2.76 per person per day. That is now increased to $6.29. In our public hospitals for people who are going to be in for just a few days and then released we are now spending $10.77 a day compared with $4.08 in 1943.
I think the minister must not be allowed to get away with his proposal to bar over half the sick people in Canada from the superior benefits which will be provided as soon as a national hospital plan comes into existence. When we are spending only $2.70 per person per day for the mentally ill, $6.29 per person per day for people in tuberculosis hospitals and $10.70 per person per day for
6516	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare people in our public hospitals I think a great injustice is being done to over halt of our sick population.
I can think of no good reason for the minister to exclude this large group except that people would demand and expect to have better care under a national hospital insurance program. Before the minister can expect to have an agreement from the provinces in connection with this important development I think he must be prepared to recommend that the benefits which he proposes to extend to the provinces to provide care for the sick should be available to all the sick. Surely we are not going to have one law for people in one type of hospital and a different law for people in another type of hospital.
I think the minister must also make more progress than he is making with a view to providing a complete medical health program for all the people in Canada. I mentioned earlier the serious problem which confronted us when war broke out. I might mention now that one of the problems which is having a very disturbing effect on our economy is the problem we have been discussing in the last few days in connection with the bill of the Minister of Finance.
I have before me a survey of physicians in Canada dated June, 1954. We find that while in Canada as a whole we have one doctor for every 971 people, in British Columbia there is one doctor for every 777 and in Newfoundland one doctor for every 2,117 people. It is possible that the people in Newfoundland are healthier than those in British Columbia, but I think the reason is that it is possible for a doctor to make a better living doing less work in a more congenial climate in British Columbia. Ontario is the only other province where the ratio is less than 1,000 people for every doctor. When disease hits the country the people living in Newfoundland are subject to plagues just as much as people living in any other part of the country. The training of doctors is now very costly, and when they graduate they are permitted to go to any part of the country or even to other countries. Therefore I submit that a complete program providing the very best health services for all the people of Canada should be accepted as a national responsibility.
The minister has put out another interesting booklet which I shall not discuss, but which I suggest hon. members should order from the very efficient research division of the department. This deals with selected public hospital and medical plans in Canada. I note that it has been necessary to draw on the province of Saskatchewan for a good deal of information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is it not true that shortly after the provincial election the hospital rates for the citizens of Saskatchewan were increased by the provincial government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I believe that is true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That has happened after every election.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I tell you frankly that that is one of our problems. If I were permitted to discuss the question which we were dealing with for the last few weeks I would mention that we have suffered real disabilities in Saskatchewan because we have had to pay a tremendous tribute as a result of tariff policies throughout the years. Corporations with head offices in Ontario and Quebec which have drained the maritimes have also drained Saskatchewan and we have had to finance a first class hospital program with the resources available in our own province. There was no way we could do it without passing the cost on to our people.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I must advise him that his time has expired.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is it not the result of the scandalously increased prices which have been permitted in this country from 1946 on? That does not sound so good.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just spoken has made some statements which in view of the importance of the subject I am afraid should not go without some explanation or some challenge. I was hoping that we could discuss this matter on the particular item. I would not want to preclude anyone, nor do I want to take advantage of anyone, but I feel that the statements the hon. member has made should be dealt with, and perhaps this is the most convenient time to deal with them though I would have preferred to wait until we get to the item.
This is the first time I have discussed in the house the proposal put forward by the Prime Minister last January on behalf of the government, at a time when I was discussing the same proposal at a meeting of all the provincial ministers of health, the provincial treasurers and representatives of our own Department of Finance in an adjoining room in this building.
That proposal is recognized by all in this house as one of the most important to have been made by the federal government in this field. It is a proposal which has been widely commented on from all sides of the house. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken referred to it in eulogistic terms, as did the

hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, particularly when he was speaking in the committee on estimates. His enthusiasm in this house has not been as generous or as vigorous as it was some months ago, but I can only conclude that that is because he has some other preoccupation in his mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is because several months have gone by and you are not getting along very well.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
On March 21 the hon. member did say in the committee on estimates, as reported on page 18 of the proceedings:
-we, of the C.C.F. group in parliament, are pleased that this step in the field of national health insurance is being taken-
And then at page 21:
The minister knows that we will support him 100 per cent against any opposition he may have to this plan-
Then at page 145:
I am glad to see this program coming into effect.
And again on the same page:
-in this commendable step which I am glad he is taking and which I support-
Then at page 178:
Is there not some way in which this committee could express its approval of the proposals made by the government to the provinces

I do not think I am being unfair to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when I say that represented then, as I am sure it does now, his acceptance of this plan. The background of this proposal lies in the fact that in May 1948 the federal government embarked upon a large program of grants in aid away and beyond the proposals made in 1945 in the matter of what has been properly characterized as a package deal covering a wide front of government activity both federal and provincial. When the prime minister of that day announced that program he said it was a prerequisite to the kind of proposal which we are now discussing.
As the hon. member for York-Scarborough pointed out, last fall the premier of Ontario felt that the time had come when the provinces should give expression to this subject and when in a spirit of co-operation between the two levels of government some definite move in this particular field should be begun. It was as a result of that and the suggestions made by other premiers that it was decided to hold a conference apart from the fiscal conference which was then in session, to see if the responsible ministers with their colleagues in treasury could not meet and generally discuss this whole problem. We had a long conference, lasting a week, the
Supply-Health and Welfare longest dominion-provincial conference I think in history, last January when this whole matter was discussed.
The federal government took the position that we were not going to impose our views on any province. After a number of years in this portfolio I am satisfied that notwithstanding what may be the view of individual members, the only way to make progress in this field is by trying to understand the problems and responsibilities of the different levels of government and in that spirit to try to see if agreement cannot be reached.
I am sure that as a result of that view we have made great progress in the health field in this country between all the provinces without exception and the federal government. I am satisfied that if we are going to make further progress in this field that is the spirit which must animate those who have to do with any level of government. That certainly is the attitude I have taken and that I am taking tonight.
With that in mind, on behalf of the federal government I said that we had our view as to what the next step should be but we were not going to impose our view, and we would like to have the provinces tell us what they thought were the steps that should be taken, if any steps could be taken in so far as the provinces were concerned. I indicated that we were prepared now to give technical and financial support to schemes put forward by the provinces on the basis of roughly 50 per cent federal contribution and roughly 50 per cent provincial contribution, based upon 25 per cent of the national per capita cost and 25 per cent of the provincial per capita cost.
This formula would yield to the maritime provinces in particular greater proportions from the federal treasury than would be the case with certain of the western provinces, notably British Columbia and Saskatchewan, both of which provinces, by the way, through their appropriate ministers said that our formula was fair and, in the words of the provincial treasurer for Saskatchewan, that we had put forward at long last a scheme which he thought was calculated to encourage interest on the part of the provinces and which was fair to all the provinces.
The provinces then put forward unanimously, without any exception, the view that we should proceed on a stage basis, and no province insisted that we should go further than we have in the proposal before us, and that included every province without exception. The province of British Columbia did say that they would prefer a wider scheme; but they recognized that at the present time, as this situation depended on the co-operation

Supply-Health and Welfare of all provinces and the federal government, it would be impractical to try to impose upon certain provinces financial obligations which they were not prepared to assume or which they thought they could not bear. Therefore no one should suggest that the limited aspect of the program is the product of any one government, because that it not the case, as the records of the conferences would show.
The provinces suggested, and with this we agree, that the next steps in this matter should be in the fields of laboratory and radiological diagnostic services and hospital insurance. It is true that at the conference that was held in the winter the premier of Ontario proposed for study some six different stages and phases of health services which he thought should receive the embrace of the federal and provincial governments, but at that conference his spokesman joined with the other provinces in saying that they did not want at this time to deal with any other aspects than the two I have mentioned, radiological and laboratory diagnostic services and hospital insurance.
We have put forward this proposal based upon the formula that it can become effective if six provinces, representing a majority of the people of Canada, express their concurrence; and I have indicated that just as quickly as that concurrence is expressed no delay will be forthcoming legislatively on the part of the federal government. I have taken advantage of the interval between the conference in January and the present time to discuss this situation informally with certain provinces in the hope of helping them to arrive at a decision at the earliest possible date. Not very long ago I discussed this matter with the premier of Ontario. I think I can say, and I think this is the way in which I should express myself in a matter involving co-operation, that we had a useful conversation, a helpful conversation, a constructive one, the kind of co-operation, the kind of discussion which I believe is calculated to achieve results. I remain hopeful that as a result of these discussions there will not be undue delay.
I recognize, as the hon. member for York-Scarborough has said, that this is an important matter, a matter that will cost the federal government in the first year a minimum of $182 million with a total national expenditure of almost $400 million, a matter that quite properly should be considered with care by every government concerned. The province of Ontario has established now a hospital commission with a very eminent hospital administrator, Mr. Swanson, as chairman. While its existence is not predicated 
upon the necessary acceptance of this proposal, it would seem to me that the implications in the announcement of the commission are clear that the commission would not have been established if the government of Ontario was not giving sympathetic and serious consideration to the proposal which the federal government has made in this field.
The federal government will have to decide through its Minister of Finance, speaking on behalf of the government in terms of what the budgetary policy in this particular will be, but I can say that under no circumstances is it the intention of the federal government in any way to impose any condition on any province as to how it has to raise its portion of the sharing plan. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre expressed the hope, if I understood him rightly, that we would see to it that this would be on a contributory basis, and that we would see to it that the provinces embarked upon schemes with that principle in mind. I can only say that as far as the federal government is concerned we have indicated to the provinces that we attach no conditions as to how they raise their share of the program; and that was stated by the Prime Minister, I think, at the full conference as well.
I may express the view that contributions, as they have them in one province, are perhaps a more difficult way of realizing the program; but that would be a personal view. In the province of British Columbia they now take the money out of the consolidated revenue fund and I think the scheme there, in spite of the difficulties that attended it at first, is now working admirably. Let there be no mistake about this. The federal government is not dragging its feet on this matter, as was suggested by the hon. member for Mackenzie, and he knows better than that. I take it that was a slip of the tongue.
He knows we have put forward a proposal that was arrived at after careful consideration, a proposal that in our judgment, would have great benefits for the people of this country, a proposal which depends for its realization on acceptance by the required number of provinces. We have had three provinces, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, who after an interval, that interval being some months in the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan, have acceded to the proposal.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the table I placed before the committee on estimates, which shows the relative responsibilities of the various jurisdictions in so far as the net cost to governments of this proposal is concerned. I do not propose to go into those details now. We can do that if

necessary when we reach the item. But there is something I do want to say, and it is one of the main reasons I rose to my feet at this time. I did not want it to go out to the country that this proposal was giving preference to one group of sick people as opposed to another. The hon. member for Mackenzie said that we were excluding mental patients and tuberculosis patients. That is the same argument he made in the committee on estimates. Notwithstanding my answers he persists in making that statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Has the policy been
changed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The fact is this. In every province of Canada but one the total cost of mental health care and of tuberculosis care is borne out of provincial revenues. It is not borne by the individual patient himself. The only exception to that, in terms of the provinces, is the province of Ontario. There the burden is over 90 per cent; that is the burden borne by the province, not by the individual patient. In other words, patients who are suffering from mental illness in the province of Ontario, to the extent of over 90 per cent, receive medical care and treatment for that illness at the expense of all of the taxpayers of the province. The individual does not pay for these services. That is the case in every other province, only to a larger extent. This is not a scheme to subsidize provincial governments-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Is the minister not wrong?
Saskatchewan does that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes. I said every province except Ontario; and there it is 90 per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Has the minister checked in respect of Manitoba? I think he was wrong about that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No; they told us the same thing at the conference.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the minister checks, I think he will find that he is wrong.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
They gave us this information at the conference; that is the information I have given to you.
The point I am trying to make is this. This is a proposal for hospital insurance to assist the individual in meeting his costs of hospital care. It is not a proposal put forward to relieve the provincial governments of responsibilities which normally they have accepted and which they continue to accept. It is a proposal made to assist individuals in meeting the cost of hospital care. Any individual who is suffering from tuberculosis or from mental illness and who is receiving treatment in a general hospital is included
Supply-Health and Welfare in the scheme; and he should be included in that scheme because in those cases the individual is called upon to bear the hospital cost himself, not the province. The province does not give assistance in those cases. That kind of individual should be embraced by this proposal.
So the statement that has been made by the hon. gentleman is not a fair one. I am not criticizing the hon. gentleman unduly. I just think that in a matter of this importance he would want to join me in making sure that what I have said is correct. To show that the position we are taking is a proper one may I say this. No hon. gentleman can point to any jurisdiction in any country in the world, except in the case of the United Kingdom, where tuberculosis and mental patients are covered by the hospital insurance scheme. The reason they are covered in Britain is that the hospitals there now belong entirely to the state. In Canada I do not think anyone seriously proposes that the title to our hospitals should be transferred from religious or private bodies to the state, either in the name of the federal government or of the provincial government.
In any event, this government does not propose to enter into any scheme whereby we would take over the ownership of hospitals. There is not one jurisdiction in the world, including the province of Saskatchewan and the province of British Columbia, where the cost of tuberculosis and mental care is covered by the hospital insurance program. In the province of Saskatchewan there is a separate account. The cost of mental illness and the cost of tuberculosis care in that province, in British Columbia and in Alberta, is borne by the province out of the consolidated fund. It is not covered by the hospital insurance scheme.
In asking that we should do something the provinces themselves do not do, or do something that no other jurisdiction in this field does, my hon. friend is simply asking us to use a device to give further grants not to individuals but to the provincial governments themselves. I can tell my hon. friend this. Whatever he may think about us on this side, that is assuming a measure of naivete which I do not think even an active critic like the hon. member could possibly justify, and so we are not going to do what he urges. But let me make it clear that individuals who bear the cost of mental illness care and of tuberculosis care and who are in general hospitals will be embraced by this scheme.
I do not intend at this stage, Mr. Chairman, to deal with the other points that were brought up except to say to my friend the
6520	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that he may find it convenient to make all these proposals involving considerable sums of money. However, I should like to tell him this. We believe this proposal is a good one and I know he thinks so too. We should like to see it realized. One way to stop it from being realized would be to saddle the people with a burden which at this time I do not believe, on my responsibility as a minister of the crown, X should like to say they could bear.
For instance, he has proposed that we should have an enlargement of our old age security plan. I have calculated that the proposal he has made would cost another $621 million, which would mean that we would be spending on old age security at this time, if that proposal were accepted, more than is spent now in this entire department. He is asking us to spend in this one particular field twice as much money as the federal government spent on its entire account in 1938. If one were to accept hi# proposal now-which by the way does not take into account supplementary payments in British Columbia, in Saskatchewan and in Alberta-I am sure we would not have any hospital insurance scheme. If my hon. friend really believes in hospital insurance, as I believe he does, though I sometimes question the effectiveness of the methods by which he seeks to realize his objective, if he wants to stop this hospital insurance program all he has to do is to go on making extravagant demands that he knows or must know cannot possibly be met.
I say that to him. As anxious as he is, as am I and as is the government to see these things done, I ask him to realize the effect of some of his proposals. Does he think for one moment that it would be possible to persuade the people of Canada to increase appropriations in this one field by $600 million and at the same time go forward and realize the various schemes of health insurance that he has been talking about and that we have been talking about and with regard to which we are now proposing that something be done? When we come to this particular item-I hope he does not do it now, in order that we may get on with the business-no doubt my hon. friend will deal with the matter.
I simply want to conclude what I have to say by saying to the hon. member for Lanark that I thought he made an admirable statement today. I have always felt that the hon. member for Lanark makes a constructive speech on this particular subject, and I thought his speech today was of a high order. I can only say to him that the


matters he covered are engaging our attention. As he knows, many of the subjects referred to by him are subjects that come within the primary competence of the provincial governments. However, under the grants in aid program we are able to give great assistance to the provinces in these matters.
Finally I would simply say this with regard to the hospital proposal, the government has made this proposal one that has no strings attached to it except that the plan should be universally applied, that it should not be given to one class and not to another. That is the only condition we have put forward. I am hoping this, and I am not saying it in a narrow political sense, because I know what are the responsibilities of the provinces. I can only say in the name of the federal government that we are hoping the provincial governments will be able to give their acceptance to this proposal as quickly as possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have one or two matters I should like to bring before the minister, Mr. Chairman. I should like to bring all of them before him at the one time, because in that way I will save your time, I will save my own time and I will save the time of the committee.
The first matter is the one which has just been discussed by the minister, the T.B. patients. I am not going into the problem of who pays for them. I know the province does that. We have built the finest hospitals in Canada, we take these people in and restore them to good health. After they have been in there two years, the doctor looks them over and says, "Now, you are getting on well and you can go home." He says, "Get a light job". Are there any light jobs for such people? I think all the jobs available are heavy jobs.
Then if an Indian who has T.B. comes down to Winnipeg or Selkirk he goes into the hospital for a year or two. When it is time for him to go home he is told to get a light job. He does not do anything, because there are no light jobs. He has to eat, so he goes to the Indian agent, and what does the doctor tell him? He tells him to live on a light diet and here is what the Indian agent gives him: 38 pounds of flour; five pounds of lard; one and a half pounds of tea; four pounds of sugar; a box of matches; two and a half pounds of baking powder; five pounds of beans; two pounds of cheese; seven pounds of salt bacon-that is not the kind of bacon we get on our breakfast table, that is sow belly-five pounds of rice; two and a half pounds of. table salt.

Here is a man who has been in the hospital for two years, and they give him that sort of diet on which to live. This can be remedied. A doctor can issue an order so he will get more nourishing food. There is no milk included in this diet, and I believe a sick man should get milk. However, I leave that to the doctors to decide. There should be some law by means of which these people would be taken care of in that period, because we make them better in these hospitals that cost a lot of money and then they are back again six months after we let them out, perhaps as bad as ever. I say, don't waste money in that way.
Now, you know, you have a very fine hospital at Norway House, but you cannot get service there because there is the break-up and the freeze-up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend think I was unfair if I suggested that when we come to the item on Indians we could deal with this particular question? What is the responsibility of the federal government in connection with retarded school children? Will the minister write and tell me?

Supply-Health and Welfare

speechtext: The minister will let me know about that? I know the provincial government is still adding schools to take care of these children, but there do not seem to be enough. I wondered if the federal government contributed any money?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have a few remarks to make of a general nature. First, let me say I was going to bring up the matter of old age pensions, but in view of what the minister has said I shall reserve my comments on that until we get to the item. Let me say I have no intention of unduly holding up the minister, because I know he has two very big jobs on his hands. One of his jobs is this department, which I consider is probably the most important department in the entire government. Then he has been picked by Canada, because he is Canada's ace peacemaker, to deal with the Russians in regard to disarmament. I personally believe that we will never have a really substantial increase in the old age pensions, family allowances and so on, until we do make a very drastic reduction in our expenditures on armaments. We cannot make a drastic and worth-while reduction in armaments unless we have a world agreement on disarmament. So I say everybody who really wants a better welfare set-up in Canada should do everything possible to send down to New York again our ace peacemaker, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Now, in my opinion, and I have given a great deal of study to this as well as visiting a good many of the countries myself, Canada has the best balanced welfare system of any country, at least in our part of the world. I regard the proposal for the first stage of the national health insurance scheme as the most important proposal that has been made, even by this government all down through its long record of achievement in the welfare field.
Tonight during the supper hour I was reading some of the history of the introduction of family allowances into this house. I am glad I did take the time to read it, because I found that I was doing a great injustice in my own mind to the Conservatives.
6522	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare
I had always thought all the Conservatives had opposed family allowances right down to the time of the vote, but when I read Hansard for 1943 and 1944 I found that all but one of the Conservatives in this house at that time did vote for family allowances. While it is true that one of the very ardent Conservatives from Toronto was temporarily suspended from the house because of the ardour of his opposition to family allowances, that was the beginning of the agreement of the whole party, because the whole party except one did vote for family allowances on that particular day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That was not the reason the hon. member was suspended.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am glad to say that down through the years there has been manifested from time to time by all those in this house an appreciation of what national health insurance would mean for this country. For instance, last year I think we all received a great thrill, certainly I did, when the man temporarily leading the opposition, the veteran member for Dufferin-Simcoe, surprised us all by coming out for health insurance at the tail end of his speech in the debate on the speech from the throne. When I look back in Hansard, as I did in my search today, I see that the present acting leader of the opposition, my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, asked this question at page 5472 of Hansard of 1944, volume VI:
Then, what about health insurance? We were led to believe last year that a health insurance measure was shortly to be placed upon the statute books of Canada. Well, a committee was set up, and a draft health insurance bill was placed before it; not even having the endorsement of the government, but simply presented by a department of the government. That bill was considered all last session, and this year we have had the same procedure. Another bill has been thrown to that special committee-known as the committee on social security-and has been mulled over. But we are to provide for no health insurance in Canada at this session.
What I am pointing out, of course, is that as early as 12 years ago the prominent members of the Conservative party were pushing this government for health insurance. I ask, what is the reason for the strange paralysis that seems to have overtaken the Conservative party in this house and in the country during the past few weeks? We heard the premier of Ontario, as late as the conference of last autumn, pressing the federal government to go ahead with health insurance, and then finally we have the Prime Minister of Canada laying down the conditions on which this government will recommend to this parliament federal participation in national health insurance.


I should think those terms would be endorsed not only by every fair-minded member in this house, but also by every fair-minded citizen in the whole Dominion of Canada. The federal authority was to spend $185 million a year to go in with the provinces on what amounts to a fifty-fifty scheme, with the provinces left free to decide in their own way just how they would handle it; but the strange thing is this. Three provinces have already agreed to go ahead. Three of the necessary six, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, which have different types of governments, have already agreed to go ahead.
In terms of practical politics it means this. Unless Ontario agrees to go ahead it is impossible in the foreseeable future to get sufficient governments with sufficient populations to meet the very fair stipulation laid down by the Prime Minister of Canada. Therefore, I ask, why the strange lethargy on the part of the premier of Ontario; why the strange silence on the part of the premier of Ontario? Certainly when the great pipeline crisis was on the premier of Ontario took a very forthright stand on the side of the right. Why, when this great chance for a great social advance comes along, and when the attitude of the government of Ontario is so crucial, why do we get this strange delay?
I must say that as a member of parliament from British Columbia I have a very real and immediate interest in the accession of Ontario to this scheme. I certainly hope that Ontario does not continue much longer to hold up the whole procession toward adequate social progress in this great Dominion of Canada because we, as the minister pointed out in his evidence before the estimates committee at page 124, are in this position. This is what the minister said before that committee; here is how the provinces would make out:
So that Saskatchewan would have on the positive side some $9 million, British Columbia, $8-9 million, Newfoundland, $1-8 million and Alberta, $800,000.
In other words, if and when this plan goes through-and it will not go through until Ontario ceases to fail to co-operate-we in British Columbia will immediately benefit to the tune of almost $9 million a year without any further contribution on our part from any source whatsoever.

Mr. Chairman, tonight I was surprised to hear the hon. member for York-Scarborough in bringing forward the point he was trying to present take such a circuitous route to approach it. It seems to be the same point the hon. member for Vancouver South arrived at concerning the probability of Premier Frost of Ontario accepting the national health plan brought forward by the government.
I was perfectly satisfied to let the matter rest after hearing the explanation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. His explanation was reasonable and acceptable. He pointed out that all the provinces in the dominion were very interested and co-operating with the federal government, and it was collaborating to the extent of trying to make the bill one which could be acceptable to all the provinces. He indicated that the federal government was not putting the provinces in a position where they would have to accept. The same thing is being done, apparently, as was done in the dominion-provincial tax-sharing bill. In other words the federal government is not forcing the provinces. Instead, the situation and attitude is, "If you do not like it you do not have to come in".
The situation today is that 37 years after the great Liberal party offered a national health plan as a plank in its platform, in 1919, it has finally brought it in. It did not bring it until after Premier Frost of Ontario had gone into a comprehensive and exhaustive study of the subject. As the Minister of National Health and Welfare said, Ontario has six different plans, but none are

Supply-Health and Welfare acceptable at the present time. However, the government of Ontario had a plan and was prepared to launch it, if the federal government was not prepared to do so. That is the *only reason the federal government has brought down this bill. It is because the province of Ontario brought one down and is willing to go ahead with it. Now the members of the government are standing up here and saying, "Where does Ontario stand on this matter?" Ontario is ready to give the lead any time but it is the same old story; this government has brought in a bill that has conditions attached to it.
As far as government public buildings are concerned, it will pay taxes under certain conditions. As far as dominion-provincial agreements are concerned, there are certain conditions attached. This government always brings in a jug-handled deal and usually a short-change bill as far as Ontario is concerned. The government tries to make Ontario the goat. Why does it not concentrate on bringing other provinces in instead of Ontario? Ontario will give you the leadership if you want it..

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext: It is bad enough that you stop the opposition; don't stop your own men.

If it does not inconvenience the minister I might proceed with it now, unless the minister would care to give me a little more latitude later on when we are discussing some of the items.

speechtext:

rMr. Small.]

speechtext: With that reservation I am quite satisfied.

speechtext:
I am going to preface my
remarks by saying I do not intend to speak at any great length, and I hope the minister will not take any of my time in trying to persuade me to defer what I have to say.
I waited with interest for the reply that might be forthcoming to the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver South in respect to action that might be taken by Ontario to facilitate what we hope to see in British Columbia. I am in complete sympathy with that aspect of the hon. member's discussion, but I must say I was rather disappointed at some of his earlier remarks when he dragged in the old bogey about an increase in the old age pension being dependent on some reduction in arms expenditures.
In this connection I notice that the minister -I am going to get mixed up in his title like the hon. member for Vancouver South did-* the Minister of National Health and Welfare-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Wealth and hellfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: -'did not suggest that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre earlier today had made a slip of the tongue when he put forth his proposal in respect to an increase in the basic old age pension. He can say that something is being done in the field of national hospital insurance, but I certainly cannot go along with the thinking of people like the hon. member for Vancouver South and the minister who suggest that an increase in the old age pension at this time would necessarily endanger progress in the field of hospital insurance. I can understand the minister with the responsibilities of his office perhaps being a little more timid, particularly when he might have to convince some of the more timid-minded members of the cabinet-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: None of them is timid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-but I am surprised to find the hon. member for Vancouver South tagging along with that timidity.
The suggestion the minister made that this increase would cost $600 million is one I do not find the least bit appalling. I think it is a matter of having a proper appreciation of what is important, an appreciation of those things on which the people of Canada should be spending their money. I agree that $600 million sounds like a lot of money, but to me in terms of the plain economics of the productive capacity of the Canadian people, $600 million is not a great sum. It might mean that some people in this country could possibly not afford a new car quite as often, or perhaps they could not turn in their old television set for the latest model as frequently,

but I believe a proper appreciation of the values involved would indicate that even if some people had to make minor sacrifices of that kind the $600 million would be much better spent in the field of old age pensions. I certainly would not agree that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was the least bit unrealistic when he put forward his proposal.
I would like to tell the minister a little story concerning something that happened to me last fall. I was invited to attend a banquet of an old age pensioners' organization. I felt this was a strictly non-political gathering and I made what I considered to be a nice little speech appropriate to the occasion. I very carefully avoided becoming too fervent in any expression of my own particular views on the subject of what should be done concerning an increase. I found myself with mingled feelings of consternation and delight when a little later on in the proceedings one of the women in attendance, who I happen to know is the president of the Liberal women's association in the district, got up and made a very forthright speech on the subject of what should be done about old age pensions.
I only wished I had a tape recorder there so I could play her speech here for the benefit of the minister at this time, because I am sure no words of mine could be as forthright in expressing the requirements in this connection as her words were. I am completely confident that the majority of people-at least those in my own constituency-would be quite prepared to support a proposal to increase the old age pension in something like the degree suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
It seems to be that if this great Liberal party with its huge majority in this parliament had a bit more courage and would take that kind of issue to the people of this country, they would be more likely to prolong the life of this government than if they hang back with their present timidity in this field. I think it is time to go out and tell the people of Canada that an increase in old age pensions is going to cost money. Let us not try to hide the fact that these things do cost money. Let us go out and say that in the kind of society in which we feel we should be living, this is the sort of thing we should be spending our money on instead of on some of these highly advertised, unnecessary gadgets which we find in the country today.
This is all I intend to say on this particular subject, but there is one other point with which I should like to deal while I am on my feet. I have made previous reference
Supply-Health and Welfare to this question, and I should like to make a special plea for a specific guiding allowance for the blind persons of Canada.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend be prepared to deal with that when we come to the particular item covering blindness allowances?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall co-operate with the minister to that extent. He knows I have an interest in this matter.

speechtext: I shall be glad to deal with it then.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Before the item carries I should like to ask the minister a specific question. This is the occasion on which he is officially before the committee, but there are certain matters which I wish to discuss with him pertaining to his performance at the United Nations. Will he be appearing in a capacity in which I can ask those questions at a later date? Will he be prepared to explain what he did in respect to the package deal he worked out last year? I shall refrain from asking any questions now pertaining to that matter, on the understanding that he is making a special commitment to be here so I can ask him these questions at a later time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, during the past two or three years there have been a number of times when hon. members on this side of the house have asked the minister questions on the orders of the day and he has spent a great deal of time eulogizing his party and the great program they have undertaken. He has given the impression generally throughout the country over the years that this was just about the most perfect thing that ever happened in a most perfect world, and everything was shipshape. However, that is far from the truth in the case of old age pensions of $40 per month on which people of 70 years of age and over are asked to live.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me, as an old-time room-mate who lived in the same house, to suggest that we could discuss that on the particular item?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the minister will give the same kind of long dissertation as he gave on health.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is the minister prepared to give it now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When we get on the item.

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are a number of things I would like the minister to talk about when we come to that. I can list a few of them. He may try to place the blame on the increased cost of living, but I would like him to explain how we can expect old age pensioners to have a better standard of living today on $40 a month than they had 15 years ago when the cost of living was about half what it is today.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: When we come to that item I shall be happy to deal with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are you going to deal with the matter?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Only three minutes to hold it up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I will not take as long as the hon. member for Vancouver South, and I shall try to deal with matters having to do with the department of wealth and hellfare, when people of 70 years of age are asked to live on this amount. The cost of living is striking these people so hard that it is just utterly impossible for them to carry on. This will require a lot of explaining, and I hope the minister will have something more than words to give us. What I want to see is something in the way of action in giving assistance to people who have to live on $40 a month. The hon. member for Mackenzie referred to an article in a Toronto paper where a reporter outlined his experience trying to live on $40 a month. It brings things pretty close to home.
We read in the paper that the cost of living index had gone up 1-2 points, but that was let go by almost without a gesture or statement by the government. The great part of that increase was made up by the increased cost of food. It is costing the older people more for the food they have to buy, while the producers in my part of the country find that their returns are going down. The Minister of Agriculture knows that.
There is something wrong about the way we are forcing and compelling these people to live when the cost of living continues to

go up. There is absolutely nothing being done to help people who are absolutely helpless and able to do nothing about it except wait for their cheque for $40 at the end of the month. The first statutory item under the minister's estimates is for $17,000 for himself, which is quite a bit more than the $40 per month the old age pensioner gets. Under the present system, when the minister reaches 70 years of age he will have that added to the $17,000, provided he is still minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Heaven forbid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not know how many years he has to go. This matter is far too important to be glossed over when we are dealing with this department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We will be coming to the item dealing with old age pensions, when we can have a full discussion.	.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The only difficulty about that is I may be called out to a committee meeting. The committees could have been sitting in January, February and March. I asked the chairman of one committee when the committee was going to sit and he just said, "How high is up?" May I call it ten o'clock?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the hon. member not agree to leave this until we come to the item, so we can pass the general item? We have had a very full general discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
